item.title: AI Surveillance Startup Flock To Cut Several Hundred Jobs Amid Backlash, Sources Say
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Reuters reports:
Flock plans to let go of about 18% of its employees, people with direct knowledge of the plans said on Thursday, as the maker of AI-powered surveillance cameras and license-plate readers faces mounting opposition to its products from communities and lawmakers....
The company has about 1,500 employees [with job cuts hitting 270 employees]. Flock faces growing scrutiny from regulators, lawmakers, and privacy advocates, despite drawing strong investor interest among venture capitalists. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed Americans are divided on whether Flock cameras are a good idea. Some 38% of the country supports the use of Flock cameras in their community, compared to 47% who oppose their use.
A related story... In Texas this week a county commissioner decommissioned all 61 of their Flock surveillance cameras and license plate readers, according to a local news report. County residents "have raised serious questions about who can access this data, what vendors can disclose, improper searches, and records being kept after data expires," the precinct's Chief Public Affairs Officer said.

item.title: GPT 6 Astra - Will It Shake Up the World of Marketing?
item.author: Vipin Labroo
item.content:encoded: The launch of GPT -6 Astra by OpenAI promises to forever alter the way marketing has been approached and carried out hitherto. Far from being a mere content creation tool, it is an autonomous marketing entity capable of performing like a human digital assistant that can glide between desktop apps, fill out forms, and take charge of workflows. This path-breaking ability dubbed “computer use” empowers marketers across the board in a seminal manner. Some are claiming that GPT6 Astra rivals the AI holy grail, AGI or Artificial General Intelligence.It transforms content creation by going beyond creating drafts and outlines. Astra goes several steps ahead, taking care of research, creating customised versions of content, and disseminating it across formats and channels entirely autonomously.It gives a leg up to the search strategy, moving it from keyword use to achieve SEO and aligning it with GEO (Generative Engine Optimisation) and AEO (Answer Engine Optimization), thereby making it possible for brand content to be cited as part of AI-summarized search results.Marketers are rid of the necessity of having to manually navigate between CRM data, creating ad content, and buying media space and time. Astra-enabled computer use makes all that a thing of the past by enabling multi-app complex workflows.With Astra being able to operate a computer the way a human does, with its ability to click, type, navigate between desktop apps, and essentially take the task in question to conclusion, it is a must-have for savvy marketers as it helps them respond to comprehensive customer queries that ask for a simple and straightforward answer that best speaks to their needs.In the past, all their search queries resulted in a long list of links that they were expected to open and do their own detailed research. In the case of AI-powered research, customers are much more likely to click on the two or three well-recommended links as they know that these have been thoroughly well-researched and speak optimally to their needs.Increasingly, people base their buying behavior on the basis of their AI chats. Astra helps marketers by turbocharging this process in terms of its speed, allowing for a level playing field to businesses across scale and size. That being stated, marketers will no longer be able to leverage high-quality generic content to engage with their prospects, as everyone will be on to it. What they will now have to do is prove the genuineness of their claims by furnishing tangible and credible evidence.Real people talking about real achievements will cut ice; grandiose announcements by way of highly well-crafted content will no longer be accepted at face value. AI citing too happens not on the basis of content volume or how professionally it is created but by a real example of a claim being validated by a person of stature vouching for it, or by way of demonstrating it via a case study or a well-regarded research paper.Ironically, what Astra does is not make human intervention irrelevant, but in fact makes them the final arbiter about the type of content that finally goes out. It is the human touch and its authentic stamp of approval that makes content resonate with the intended target audience. Your voice has to be heard.

item.title: ALLOX TGE Nears With 363K Eligible Claimants and Coinbase-Owned Sonar Sale
item.author: Crypto Unfolded
item.content:encoded: The upcoming ALLOX token generation event (TGE) is shaping up to be a major milestone for the AI-powered capital allocation platform, with 363,298 users eligible to claim tokens, more than 2.6 million registered wallets and a $1 million public sale launching through Coinbase-owned Sonar.AlloX has , revealing that 1,807 participants joined its private round, while 583 registered for the public sale within the first 24 hours. Another 86,290 KYC-verified users participated in the project's exclusive Binance Wallet Booster campaign.The numbers highlight the scale of AlloX's community ahead of token distribution. The platform also reports approximately 150,000 average daily users, more than $56 million invested on-chain and over $161 million in cumulative DEX aggregator volume.Registration for the is open, with commitments scheduled to begin on October 12, 2026. The offering uses Sonar by Echo, the on-chain token sale infrastructure acquired by Coinbase in a $375 million deal.Meanwhile, ALLOX has established a pre-market trading presence on Aspecta, adding an early price-discovery venue ahead of its official token launch.More Than 363,000 Users Eligible for ALLOX TGE DistributionAlloX's token generation event will activate a distribution process involving hundreds of thousands of eligible participants from the project's earlier campaigns and funding rounds.The project has confirmed 363,298 users eligible to claim ALLOX, subject to applicable vesting arrangements. This includes a broader rewards ecosystem developed through platform campaigns, community participation and token allocation programs.The launch follows months of activity across AlloX's AI portfolio platform, which allows users to create diversified, risk-managed crypto baskets based on market narratives and investment preferences.Its public tokenomics establish a total supply of 1 billion ALLOX, with 35% allocated to the community and 30% designated for ecosystem development.The token's launch also marks the next phase of AlloX's product roadmap, which includes staking pools, premium feature access, community governance, protocol integrations and public API access.These planned features extend the role of ALLOX beyond the initial distribution event, connecting the token to the platform's developing ecosystem of on-chain capital allocation services.The exact TGE date and final token distribution schedule have not yet been announced. has confirmed that the event will not take place immediately after the public sale closes.Coinbase-Owned Sonar Hosts $1 Million ALLOX Public SaleA central component of the TGE preparations is the $1 million public offering conducted through Sonar, the token fundraising infrastructure developed by Echo.Founded by prominent crypto investor Cobie, Echo enables projects to raise capital directly from investors, while Sonar provides the infrastructure for self-hosted public token offerings.AlloX is using Sonar for its public round, connecting its fundraising process to Coinbase-owned technology ahead of TGE.The introduce three allocation plans with different valuations and token release schedules:Silver: $0.065 per ALLOX at a $65 million fully diluted valuation, with 100% unlocked at TGE.Gold: $52 million FDV, with 20% unlocked at TGE and the remaining 80% vesting linearly over 12 months.Platinum: $39 million FDV, with a three-month cliff followed by 12 months of linear vesting and no initial TGE unlock.Participants can commit between $100 and $200,000 per entity using USDC or USDT on Ethereum.All allocations require identity verification through Sonar, including KYC for individuals and KYB for businesses. Oversubscribed commitments will be distributed pro rata, with unallocated funds automatically refunded during settlement.The offering establishes three distinct entry valuations before ALLOX becomes available through its official token distribution.Binance Wallet Campaign Delivered 86,290 Verified ParticipantsAlloX's TGE preparations follow a completed milestone within the Binance Wallet ecosystem.The project became the first to conduct an exclusive campaign under Binance Wallet's Booster format, distributing rewards from a pool of 10 million ALLOX tokens.Promoted through an , the campaign attracted 86,290 KYC-verified participantswho engaged with wallet connections, AI portfolio construction and other on-chain activities.AlloX's public-sale website states that the project was selected as one of 20 participants from a pool of more than 650 Binance Alpha tokens for the exclusive Booster initiative.The campaign gives ALLOX an established presence within Binance Wallet's early-stage token ecosystem. A separate Binance Alpha trading debut or Binance spot listing would require an official exchange announcement.The verified participation figures now contribute to a considerably larger token-launch audience, with the project reporting millions of registered wallets across its platform.ALLOX Pre-Market Activity Adds to TGE MomentumALLOX is already represented in pre-market trading through Aspecta Pre-Market V3, allowing traders to establish exposure ahead of the official token generation event.The token's has drawn attention to the relationship between secondary-market valuations and the public-sale terms.Early October trading observations placed ALLOX around an $80 million implied fully diluted valuation, above the $65 million valuation offered to Silver public-sale participants.At that valuation, the difference represents approximately a 23% premium over the Silver round.The premium is a historical pre-market observation, not a guaranteed TGE price or return. Pre-market instruments operate under different settlement and liquidity conditions, while Gold and Platinum public-sale allocations carry additional vesting restrictions.Even so, ALLOX has entered price discovery before its token launch, providing a reference point alongside the three published sale valuations.AlloX Enters TGE With $5 Million in Strategic Backing and an Operating ProductBeyond its public sale and token distribution, AlloX has developed an operating AI-powered capital allocation platform since launching in February 2026.The platform translates market narratives into diversified token portfolios through automated allocation strategies, combining artificial intelligence with decentralized trading and risk-management tools.Its services span BNB Chain, Base, Ethereum and Robinhood Chain, supporting an expanding range of on-chain assets and investment themes.AlloX reports more than 19.1 million transactions, $56.67 million invested on-chain and $161.45 million in DEX aggregator volume. Approximately 78.1% of tracked portfolios show positive profit and loss, a reported performance snapshot rather than a guarantee of future returns.The project has also secured substantial strategic investment.Security assessments add another element to its operating record. gives AlloX an A-grade score, with its published audit recording zero critical findings and 11 resolved issues out of 13 identified.The product's operational history, reported user growth and investment base distinguish the ALLOX TGE from a token launch built solely around a fundraising announcement.MiCA White Paper Establishes Kraken Trading ObjectiveThe white paper names Payward Global Solutions Limited, Kraken's European trading-platform entity, in connection with AlloX Ltd.'s intention to seek admission to trading.The disclosure establishes a documented Kraken trading objective for ALLOX, although it does not represent a confirmed listing approval or trading date.Kraken's European entity operates under the EU Markets in Crypto-Assets framework, while AlloX's white paper provides the relevant crypto-asset disclosures for its intended market activities.The published regulatory documentation joins the project's completed Binance Wallet campaign and Coinbase-owned Sonar offering among the concrete developments preceding its token generation event.October 12 Public Sale Marks the Next Step Toward ALLOX TGEAlloX's immediate focus is the opening of public-sale commitments on October 12.Eligible participants can register at , connect their wallet, complete Sonar identity verification and select their allocation before submitting funds during the active sale window.Commitments are final once submitted, although they can be increased. Geographic restrictions and wallet screening requirements apply, and the team has emphasized that all participation must take place through the official portal.The TGE will follow on a separately announced schedule.With 363,298 eligible token claimants, 86,290 Binance Wallet campaign participants, 2.6 million registered wallets, over $5 million in strategic backing and an established pre-market trading venue, ALLOX is approaching its token launch with a substantial reported user base and an already operating product.The Coinbase-owned Sonar sale now serves as the next confirmed milestone before AlloX begins its wider token distribution.

item.title: Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen Is Great, But At a Cost
item.author: Richard Wakeling
item.content:encoded: Capcom choosing the exact same subtitle for two separate expansions in two different games makes a lot of sense. Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is not only a thematically relevant title, but thanks to the first game's expansion of the same name, it also conveys to longtime fans what to expect: namely, a new gameplay cycle focused on reworked loot and plenty of dungeon crawling. The key difference this time around is that instead of heading into the labyrinthine depths of a cursed island, you've got an entirely new region to explore. As someone who loved Dragon's Dogma 2, I couldn't really ask for much more. Yet changes to some of the game's core systems also dilute what made it so unique when it launched back in 2024. I know it's always been a fairly divisive game, and these changes are intended to make the experience more approachable, but they also strip away some of its magic in an effort to appeal to more people. Dark Arisen is still a great expansion, transporting you to a fascinating new region with more loot to earn, fantastical beasts to slay, and stories to behold, but it also shifts Dragon's Dogma 2 in a slightly different direction. To start with, Dark Arisen alleviates some of the game's intentional friction by reducing how often you need to travel on foot. The Eternal Ferrystone was already added to the game a few months ago, letting you freely fast travel to any portcrystal without expending a scarce resource. Those same portcrystals are located at every key location in Dark Arisen's new Norgan region. You still have to reach them on foot first to activate them, but once you do, you can simply teleport from one side of the map to the other. Using the Eternal Ferrystone is entirely optional; you can still traverse almost all of Norgan on foot if you desire, so the friction is still there if you want it. However, Dark Arisen also feels designed with unlimited fast travel in mind. The first settlement you come across, for instance, acts as a hub of sorts, letting you manage your gear, rest at the inn, and pick up a fair few side quests, so you're intended to return here often. Meanwhile, many quests require you to visit the same locations over and over again to speak with specific characters. Heading off on foot might be an option, but it's never incentivized and feels antithetical to how it wants you to play. I'm not a fan of this change. I can acknowledge that giving players more choice is a positive, but the back-and-forth quest design and reliance on fast travel means you never really feel like you have options when traversing Norgan. This has a fairly significant knock-on effect, too: Without embarking on foot more often, I rarely stumbled into the emergent moments that made the base game so thrilling. And without that palpable sense of adventure, Dark Arisen feels less like Dragon's Dogma and more like any number of action-RPGs, rendering this a fundamental change to its identity, rather than an improvement.When Dragon's Dogma 2 launched, traveling the regions of Vermund and Battahl felt treacherous, especially in the black of night. The world was as hazardous as the enemies you encountered, and campsites provided a welcome respite on your weary travels. Now, those feelings of everpresent danger and welcome safety are mostly gone. There's no risk when you can freely fast travel out of danger or skip a journey entirely. The game's uncompromising design has been softened to broaden its appeal. The same goes for changes to its save system. By letting you roll back to a manual "Interim Save" at any time, there's no longer any risk involved in your decision-making. You won't have to live with the consequences of accidentally angering a bunch of guards in Battahl's jail or fret over when to use the Unmaking Arrow. This one-hit-kill item still triggers an autosave as soon as it's fired, creating tension the moment you decide to draw back the bowstring, but the ability to select an earlier save robs it of its finality. If these changes were strictly tied to Dark Arisen, they wouldn't be quite as detrimental. Yet this sanding down of its intentional friction affects the base game, too.By changing these systems, Capcom has fundamentally altered what made Dragon's Dogma 2 so fantastic. The emergent moments that happened on the road, the interplay between its systems and physics engine, and the need to deal with the consequences of your actions--all of this combined to make the base game an unpredictable and powerful adventure that stood apart from other similar games. I enjoyed its resolute design because it forced me to tackle the world on its own terms, providing a challenge that captured a rousing sense of adventure. I still thoroughly enjoyed Dark Arisen, despite these changes, but there's also this nagging feeling that something's missing. Norgan, for its part, has moments where that classic Dragon's Dogma abrasiveness returns. The frigid region offers a nice change of pace from the verdant forests and arid deserts explored previously, with jagged, snow-capped cliffs; frozen rivers; icy tundras; and dilapidated, long-abandoned castles. The hyperboreal climate doesn't just provide a visual shift, either; the weather can be both an ally and a foe. Sudden blizzards blanket the screen in heavy snowfall, obscuring your view within a few feet and taking the mini-map out of action. You also can't fast travel during these intense whiteouts, which restores the feeling that you're battling the elements just as much as the ghouls and monsters waiting to ambush you.On the flip side, you can also use the environment to your advantage, knocking down giant overhead icicles to crush your foes, throwing and skewering them on pointy shards of ice, and rolling boulders downhill that grow larger as they pick up more and more snow. You'll appreciate the extra help when facing down demonic goatmen and abominable snowman-esque monstrosities with gnarly mouths that cover their entire torsos. At first glance, Norgan's map might seem fairly small, but there's a sprawling verticality both above and below the surface that hides its true density. New climbing hooks and grapple points have been introduced to help you tackle the elevation changes, while interconnected dungeons and caves reveal shortcuts amid expansive ancient ruins and the piles of loot therein. Speaking of which, Dark Arisen entirely reworks the game's loot system with the addition of Relics. You'll unearth this generic gear in chests and on the bodies of defeated enemies, and can then take it to one of the new vendor characters for appraisal, revealing what kind of equipment you've found, its raw stats, and, on occasion, whether it has any special attributes that enhance weapon skills or grant passive abilities. This creates a Monster Hunter-esque loop as you explore and defeat powerful foes to gather more Relics, before returning to the appraiser to reveal what you've found and upgrade your character. An unseen dice roll determines the type and quality, and no single piece of gear will remain in use for too long before you'll invariably find something better, but this is still a marked improvement over the base game's uninspired loot system--where I think I purchased more usable weapons and armor than I actually found. The base game's map has also received a similar gameplay loop of its own, with the addition of 12 repeatable dungeons known as the Lost Rite Trials. While you can easily travel back and forth between Norgan and Vermund/Battahl, these new dungeons are designed to be tackled before venturing into the snowy north, setting you up with more powerful gear to make the transition easier, with repeat visits netting more and more loot. Some of these dungeons are fairly straightforward (reach the end and kill everything along the way), while others rely on different mechanics or require prerequisites before you can enter. One such trial, which asks you to enter as either an Archer or Magick Archer, features rooms filled with support pillars you can shoot down to topple the terrain and wipe out groups of enemies. Aside from better gear, completing each Lost Rite Trial nets you an Offering Flame. These can be used at various Obelisks scattered across the frigid Norgan landscape to unlock new vocation skills and stat buffs that boost health, damage, and so on. The new skills are welcome, though bumping up the amount of skills you can equip at one time from four to six is a more notable improvement. Having more options at your disposal opens up the game's combat a tad more, and somewhat makes up for the lack of new vocations. As someone who's already maxed out most of the game's classes, though, I realize I might notice the dearth of new ones more than most.One of the more surprising things about Dark Arisen is how much I enjoyed its self-contained story. Okay, maybe "enjoyed" is the wrong word, but I was definitely more invested in seeing how things would unfold than I was in the base game. It's a solid-enough vehicle for getting you from point A to B, even if it's still just remixing themes from the first game. More characters are involved, and you spend significant time with them, so there's at least something to latch onto. The writing still has little time for subtlety or nuance, but it's appropriately broody, and the story eventually leads you to some fantastic set pieces and locations. At over 20 hours long, Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is the kind of hefty expansion we don't see very often. I might like this softened version of the game a little less than I did before, but even if some of its prickly nature has been smoothed over, Dark Arisen still offers a whole bunch more of what I loved about Dragon's Dogma 2 in the first place. For first-time players, and those returning with new hopes, it's a more approachable game, and I hope this helps it reach a broader audience. Whichever side of the divide you fall on, there's something here for both. That might sound blasphemous to some, and its vision isn't as unflinching as it was once before, but Dark Arisen--and Dragon's Dogma 2 on the whole--are still well worth your time and attention.

Epix Industries is building solutions, tools, and multiverses for the future of the professional NFT industry A girl that Rahul loved never existed in the first place HackerNoon is proud to partner with muti and Artsies Collective for the ChromaFlora Exhibition, taking place in December at the Estufa Fria in Lisbon, Portugal. The art world is a highly lucrative industry, with a reputation for being both exclusive and enigmatic. The potential cybersecurity threats that can thwart the long-awaited momentum of the online art market and how to avoid these risks. Why do I have to invest and buy some NFTs? Let's explore some objective reasons to get an NFT! The markets are down and crypto has been falling — so it’s the perfect time for artists to get to work on their next creation. Now that the online art marketplaces are finally going mainstream, how can the experience be matched to other online marketplaces? Data might be the key. Senshi is the newest NFT project that is set to disrupt the industry. This project has 5,555 unique 3D NFTs and collectibles. Senshi is the latest project that In this NFC interview, we spoke with Benjamin Agostini, Co-Founder of TheSafeBox.io. We discussed NFT art and galleries, and the future of NFTs and marketing. A look into some of the issues with OpenSea, and some of the disruptors out there providing solutions Figma has been top of its game since its launch in 2016. Global shipments of laptops, desktops, and workstations fell 21.2 percent year over year (YoY) to 58.1 million devices, the analyst said.Desktop PC shipments (including desktop workstations) decreased 23.5 percent to 11.7 million units, and laptop shipments (including laptop workstations) declined 20.6 percent to 46.4 million, per Omdia.

item.title: I Wanted a Simpler Static Site Generator, So I Created Neyx
item.author: Seyyed Ali Mohammadiyeh (Max Base)
item.content:encoded:
I have used static site generators for quite a while.Jekyll was one of the first ones that felt solid to me and the core idea still makes sense. You write some Markdown with a bit of front matter then a few layouts and after the build you end up with a site.The trouble showed up once things got bigger. Adding posts and includes and plugins and custom code and image stuff and pagination just slowed everything down. Changing a template meant saving then waiting then refreshing and it got old fast when I was tweaking CSS or layouts. Hugo is quick and there are others like Eleventy or Astro that handle the speed side better yet that was not the only thing I wanted to fix.I also wanted fewer dependencies so old projects would not break two years later when I opened them again. That is what led me to create NeyX.The requirements were simple enough. Markdown input simple templates a dev server that rebuilds on its own and plain static output at the end. Usual blog features like tags pagination RSS and search should just be there without hunting for plugins each time.At some point the build starts taking long enough that you notice it.That gets annoying pretty quickly when you are working on templates or CSS.Of course, this is not something every static site generator suffers from. Hugo is very fast, for example. There are also Eleventy, Zola, Astro, and many other tools that solve this problem in different ways.But speed was only part of what I wanted to improve.I also wanted the project itself to be simpler.Fewer dependencies. Fewer things to install. Fewer things that can stop working because I opened an old project two years later.That is what made me create NeyX.My requirements were honestly pretty basic.I wanted to write Markdown.I wanted simple HTML templates.I wanted a development server with automatic rebuilds.I wanted the generated site to be plain static files.And I wanted the usual blog features without having to install a plugin for every single one.I just did not want to build the whole toolchain around those features myself.A new NeyX project starts like this:neyx new my-blog cd my-blog neyx dev The generated directory is small:my-blog/ ├── neyx.config.yml ├── content/ ├── layouts/ ├── assets/ ├── data/ └── static/ I liked this immediately because I did not need to read much before understanding it. is your Markdown. contains the templates. is for images, CSS, and similar files. contains YAML or JSON that you want to access from templates. is for files that should simply be copied to the final output.And then there is one config file:That is pretty much the whole project structure.Routing Is Based on FilesThere is no separate routing file for normal pages.content/projects/index.md I prefer this kind of routing for blogs and documentation sites.The folder structure already tells me where the page should live. I do not really want another layer of configuration for that.A post looks like what you would expect:--- title: "Hello World" description: "My first post" date: "2026-09-24" tags: ["programming", "web"] layout: post --- # Hello World This is my first post. If you have used Jekyll, Hugo, or most other static site generators, this is familiar territory.The front matter is available in the template, and the Markdown becomes the page content.A simple layout can be very small: {{ title }}

{{ title }}

{{ & content }}
There is nothing special going on here. comes from the front matter. prints the rendered Markdown content.That is enough for a basic page.The Template Syntax Did Not Take Long to LearnOne thing that can make a static site generator annoying is its template language.I do not want to spend a day learning another DSL just to print a list of posts.NeyX keeps the syntax fairly small.Conditions look like this:{{ if description }}

{{ description }}

{{ end }}
    {{ each post in posts }}
  • {{ post.title }}
    • {{ end }}
You can include other templates:{{ include "_header.html" }} And there are filters for the usual small transformations:{{ title | truncate 50 }} There is more available, but I did not need most of it at the beginning.That is something I appreciate in tools like this.I want to learn the rest when I need it, not before I can render my first page.Development Speed Matters More Than Benchmark NumbersThis was probably my biggest frustration with some of my older static sites.People often talk about build performance in terms of milliseconds or pages per second.For me, the more important question is simpler:If I am editing a template and saving every few seconds, even a small delay becomes annoying.It builds the site, serves it locally, watches the project, and rebuilds when something changes.That is what I want from development mode.I do not want another watcher.I do not want another package just for reloads.I do not want to run three commands in three terminals to work on a blog.The development build also skips some heavier production work, such as responsive image generation, which helps keep the edit and refresh cycle fast.This sounds like a small thing, but it changes how the tool feels while you are actually using it.Production Is Just a BuildWhen I am ready to generate the final site:By default, the output goes into:That directory contains the final website.dist/ ├── index.html ├── about/ ├── posts/ ├── assets/ ├── sitemap.xml ├── feed.xml ├── atom.xml └── robots.txt At that point NeyX does not matter anymore.You can serve the result anywhere that can serve static files.That is still one of the nicest things about static sites.The build tool disappears after the build.The Built-In Stuff Is What I Ended Up Liking MostAt first I was mostly interested in the basic workflow.But after using it more, the built-in features became more interesting.A real blog usually needs more than pages.Eventually you want pagination.Then you realize the 4 MB image you uploaded should probably not be sent to every phone at full size.None of these problems is difficult.But they keep coming back.With some generators, you solve each one separately. Find a plugin. Configure it. Hope it still works after the next upgrade.NeyX handles a lot of this during a normal build.sitemap.xml feed.xml atom.xml robots.txt search-index.json api/pages.json api/posts.json That is useful because I do not have to think about most of it.tags: ["linux", "programming"] NeyX can generate pages for those tags.You can also define more taxonomy fields in the config:taxonomies: - tags - categories There is not much more to explain.And I think that is a good thing.Tags are not supposed to be an engineering project.Search Without a Search ServiceI also liked the way search works.For a personal site or documentation project, I usually do not need a full search backend.NeyX generates a static search index:Then you can add a small search UI:
    The browser loads the index and filters it locally.That is probably not what I would use for a website with millions of pages, but for a normal blog it is more than enough.No separate search server.I like solutions that match the size of the problem.Image Handling Is Built In TooImages are another place where static sites can quietly collect extra tooling.You start with a few JPEGs.Then you want smaller versions.Then you add an image script.Then that script becomes another dependency.NeyX can generate responsive variants for JPEG and PNG files in the assets directory.It can produce sizes such as:You can also skip that processing when you do not need it:This is especially useful during development when there is no reason to keep regenerating image variants after every small change. Is More Useful Than It SoundsOne command I did not expect to care much about was:It checks the generated site for problems such as broken internal links, missing assets, duplicate routes, and images without text.The nice thing about this is that static site generators can happily produce broken websites.The HTML can be perfectly valid while this link is wrong:Projects The link is still broken.before publishing is useful.It is simple, but I use tools like this more than fancy features.There Is Also a Route DebuggerIf something is going to the wrong URL, there is:It shows the routes NeyX calculated, along with the source file and layout.This is another one of those features that sounds boring until you need it.I would rather run one command than stare at my directory structure for twenty minutes.There are a few other utilities too:neyx doctor neyx info neyx benchmark checks the project setup. shows project information. runs repeated builds and reports timing.They are not things a visitor will ever see, but they make the development side nicer.The Single Binary Approach HelpsNeyX is written in Salam Programming Language and distributed as a native binary.I do not think the implementation language is the important part for most users.The useful part is the result.The project does not need a runtime just to run the generator.My mental model is basically:Markdown + YAML + HTML | NeyX | Static files That also makes deployment and CI straightforward.There is not much else to maintain.For me, that is a big part of the appeal.What About Hugo, Jekyll, Eleventy, and the Others?I do not think NeyX makes every other static site generator obsolete.That would be a silly claim.Jekyll has a huge history and still fits very naturally into the GitHub Pages ecosystem.Hugo is extremely fast and has a large community.Eleventy is flexible and works well if you are already comfortable in the JavaScript ecosystem.If I had an existing Hugo site that worked perfectly, I would not rewrite it just for fun.The reason NeyX caught my attention was simpler.I wanted something small.I wanted the usual blog features already there.And I wanted the development loop to stay fast.I was also surprised by the multilingual support.You can define languages in the config:languages: - en - fa - ar Then structure the content like this:content/ ├── en/ │ └── posts/ ├── fa/ │ └── posts/ └── ar/ └── posts/ The routes get language prefixes automatically.Templates also receive the current language and text direction, so Persian and Arabic pages can use RTL without having to manually configure each page.Translated pages can also be linked together.This is the kind of feature I might not need on every site, but when I do need it, I definitely do not want to invent the whole thing myself.The Daily Workflow Is SmallAfter using NeyX for a while, this is basically what I need to remember.neyx new post "My New Post" If the routing looks wrong:That covers most of the normal workflow.The rest is just writing Markdown and editing HTML.Which, for me, is what a static site generator should mostly get out of the way and let me do.If you want to look through the project or try it yourself, it is here:

item.title: An E-Commerce Platform Is a Reliability Problem Disguised as a Website Project
item.author: lou hackfun
item.content:encoded:
A practical guide to designing an online store that remains fast, consistent, and maintainable as catalog size, traffic, and business rules growBuilding an e-commerce site is easy to underestimate. A catalog, product page, cart, and checkout can look like a straightforward CRUD application, but the engineering constraints are very different from those of a typical content site.The moment real traffic, inventory, promotions, payments, search, user accounts, and third-party integrations appear, the system becomes a distributed application with multiple consistency boundaries.The important question is therefore not just “How do we build an online store?”How do we design an e-commerce system that stays responsive under load, keeps money and inventory correct, and remains understandable six months after launch?This article walks through that problem from an engineering perspective.1. Start With Domain Boundaries, Not FrameworksA common failure mode is choosing a stack first and defining the business model later. Frameworks are implementation details; domain boundaries are architectural decisions.A practical e-commerce platform usually contains at least these logical areas: Catalog ├── Products ├── Categories ├── Attributes └── Pricing
Customer ├── Accounts ├── Addresses └── Sessions
Commerce ├── Cart ├── Orders ├── Payments ├── Discounts └── Inventory
Platform ├── Search ├── Notifications ├── Analytics └── Admin These do not have to become separate microservices. A modular monolith can keep the same domain boundaries while deploying as one application.That distinction matters. Splitting a poorly defined codebase into ten services usually creates ten poorly defined services plus network failure modes.A good first architecture often looks like this:Browser / Mobile Client | v CDN / Edge Cache | v Web Application / API | +-----+------+---------+---------+ | | | | v v v v PostgreSQL Redis Search Queue | | +----------+-----------+ | v External Services (Payment, Shipping, Email) The design phase should make these boundaries explicit before implementation starts. For teams evaluating the product and UX layer as well as the technical layer, a practical reference is e-commerce website design, particularly when requirements include catalog structure, conversion flows, and responsive storefront behavior.2. Separate Read-Heavy and Write-Critical WorkloadsE-commerce systems have an uneven workload.Product listing pages may receive thousands of reads while inventory updates, order creation, and payment confirmation occur comparatively infrequently but require stronger correctness guarantees.That means one generic data-access strategy is usually inefficient.Typical read-heavy operations include:These are excellent candidates for caching, precomputation, and denormalized read models.The dangerous operations are different:applying a one-time couponThese operations need transactional thinking.A product page can tolerate a cache miss. A checkout operation cannot silently create two orders for one payment.3. Caching Without Creating a Consistency ProblemCaching is often introduced as a performance feature and only later treated as a data-consistency problem. In e-commerce, that order should be reversed.A useful cache hierarchy is:Browser Cache | v CDN / Edge Cache | v Application Cache (Redis) | v Database The closer the cache is to the user, the cheaper the read. The closer the system is to the source of truth, the stronger the consistency.For example, a product description can safely have a longer cache lifetime than inventory.product:{id} -> long TTL category:{id}:page -> medium TTL inventory:{sku} -> very short TTL or event-driven invalidation cart:{session_id} -> user/session scoped A good cache key should encode enough context to prevent collisions:product:v3:us:en:sku-1842 Versioning cache keys becomes especially useful during schema or serialization changes. A deployment that changes JSON shape should not accidentally deserialize stale entries created by an older version.Recent HackerNoon engineering discussions also highlight why cache layers create operational complexity rather than simply making systems “faster”; the same concerns show up in production e-commerce systems. The Many Layers of Caching is a useful companion read.4. Product Search Should Be Designed as a SubsystemSearch becomes a system of its own surprisingly early.A basic SQL query can work well at first:SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE name ILIKE '%' || :query || '%' ORDER BY popularity DESC LIMIT 20; But as requirements grow, search usually adds:At that point, forcing every concern into relational SQL becomes difficult to maintain.A more scalable architecture is:Primary DB | | domain events v Indexing Worker | v Search Index | v Search API The database remains the source of truth. The search index becomes a derived read model.This distinction is critical because search indexes can lag behind transactional data. Your application must decide what “fresh enough” means for each use case.5. Inventory Requires Stronger Guarantees Than Catalog DataInventory is where many apparently fast systems become incorrect.Suppose two customers request the final unit at nearly the same time:Customer A -> read stock = 1 Customer B -> read stock = 1 Customer A -> buy Customer B -> buy A naïve read-then-write sequence can oversell the product.One option is an atomic conditional update:UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 1 WHERE sku = :sku AND available > 0; Then verify the affected row count.row_count = 1 -> reservation succeeded row_count = 0 -> inventory unavailable This is often safer than first reading inventory and assuming the value remains valid during the next operation.For more complex reservation workflows, use a short transaction and explicitly model states such as:AVAILABLE | v RESERVED | +------> RELEASED | v COMMITTED The important point is that inventory should have a state machine, not merely an integer.6. Checkout Is a Distributed TransactionCheckout often touches multiple systems:Cart | v Inventory | v Order | v Payment Provider | v Shipping | v Email / Notifications You cannot assume that all of them succeed or fail together.Order created = success Payment authorized = success Shipping API = timeout Email API = timeout The order should not be deleted just because notification delivery failed.Instead, each operation should have its own state and retry semantics.A simplified order state machine might be:PENDING_PAYMENT | +----> PAYMENT_FAILED | v PAID | v FULFILLMENT_PENDING | v SHIPPED | v COMPLETED This is also why asynchronous messaging becomes useful. Non-critical side effects such as email, analytics, or webhook delivery can move to a queue so the customer-facing request does not depend on every external service completing synchronously.7. Idempotency Prevents Duplicate OrdersRetries are inevitable. Mobile networks fail. Browsers refresh. Users double-click. Payment gateways retry callbacks.If an operation is not idempotent, a retry can create duplicate business effects.POST /api/orders Idempotency-Key: 8b9f3a5e-... The server can store the result associated with that key:idempotency_key | +--> request fingerprint +--> response +--> status +--> expires_at If the same key is received again, the server returns the original result instead of creating another order.This pattern is especially important around payment and order creation.8. Design the Frontend Around Failure, Not Only SuccessA production UI needs more states than “loading” and “loaded”.idle loading ready refreshing empty error stale retrying Consider a category page during a temporary API failure.Showing a blank white screen communicates nothing. A better design might keep the last successful data visible and expose a recoverable error state:STALE DATA
Products shown from the last successful fetch.
[Retry] This is particularly important for e-commerce because users often reach product pages from external links, search results, campaigns, or saved bookmarks.When the interface has to support complex business rules, localized content, responsive layouts, and custom workflows, the engineering requirements should be reflected in the product-design process as well; this is where custom website development can be relevant as a broader implementation model rather than treating the storefront as a generic template.9. Observability Should Be Part of the ArchitectureA system is not production-ready merely because it works on a developer laptop.You need enough telemetry to answer questions such as:Is latency coming from the database or a third-party API?Did cache hit rate collapse after deployment?Are payment failures increasing?Are search requests timing out?Metrics - request latency - error rate - cache hit ratio - queue depth - DB connection utilization
Logs - structured JSON - correlation/request IDs - business event IDs
Traces - API -> service -> DB - API -> payment provider - API -> search service A request ID that travels through the entire stack is particularly valuable:Browser request-id: 7f42... | v API Gateway | +--> Order Service | | | +--> PostgreSQL | +--> Payment Provider Now one failed checkout can be reconstructed from a single correlation identifier.Avoid optimizing based on intuition.JavaScript execution timeThe correct optimization target is often not where developers expect it to be.For example, reducing a SQL query from 30 ms to 10 ms is irrelevant if the endpoint waits 800 ms for a slow third-party shipping API.A recent HackerNoon analysis of performance optimization at very high request volumes is a useful reminder that apparently obvious optimizations can produce unexpected trade-offs. Why “Obvious” Performance Optimizations Often Backfire explores this problem from a production-systems perspective.11. Security Is an Architectural ConstraintAn e-commerce system processes more than browsing data. It may handle personal information, addresses, order history, authentication tokens, and payment-related states.Security controls should therefore appear in the architecture itself:Browser | HTTPS + secure cookies | API | Authorization middleware | Domain services | Parameterized DB access Common implementation requirements include:parameterized database queriesCSRF protection where cookie-based authentication is usedsecure and HttpOnly cookiesserver-side authorization checkssecret management outside source controlaudit logging for sensitive administrative actionsstrict webhook signature verificationA hidden form field or frontend validation rule is not an authorization boundary. The server must enforce business permissions.12. Where a Monolith Ends and a Service Boundary BeginsMicroservices are useful when independent scaling, ownership, deployment, or fault isolation justifies the additional complexity.They are not a mandatory maturity milestone.For many stores, a well-structured modular monolith is a better first architecture:src/ catalog/ customers/ cart/ orders/ inventory/ payments/ search/ notifications/ Each module should expose clear interfaces and avoid reaching into another module's tables or internal classes without a defined contract.Later, if search needs a separate scaling profile, it can become a service because the boundary already exists conceptually.That is a healthier migration path than beginning with distributed systems merely because the architecture diagram looks impressive.13. A Practical Production ChecklistBefore calling an e-commerce platform production-ready, verify:[ ] Domain boundaries are explicit [ ] Read-heavy paths have an intentional cache strategy [ ] Inventory writes are atomic or transactional [ ] Order creation is idempotent [ ] Payment callbacks are safely retryable [ ] Search is treated as a derived read model when necessary [ ] External-service failures have bounded impact [ ] Frontend states include empty, stale, and recoverable error states [ ] Logs contain correlation IDs [ ] Key business metrics are monitored [ ] Sensitive operations are authorized server-side [ ] Database migrations are repeatable [ ] Load tests cover the checkout path [ ] Rollback/deployment procedures are documented The goal is not to maximize architectural complexity. The goal is to make the system's important guarantees explicit.A production-grade e-commerce platform is fundamentally a reliability problem disguised as a website project.The catalog can be simple. The hard parts appear when traffic increases, inventory becomes scarce, payments can timeout, search indexes lag, caches become stale, and multiple services have to participate in one customer journey.The strongest architecture is usually the one that makes these failure modes visible and manageable:Separate business domains from framework code.Optimize reads without weakening write-critical consistency.Treat caching as a consistency problem as well as a performance tool.Model inventory and checkout as explicit state machines.Make retryable operations idempotent.Design UI states around partial failure instead of only the happy path.Instrument the system before production incidents force you to.Prefer a modular monolith until there is a measurable reason to distribute it.Once those principles are in place, the choice of framework, database, search engine, hosting platform, and frontend stack becomes an implementation decision rather than an architectural gamble.References and Further ReadingDisclosure: This article includes two contextual references to AzkiWeb resources because they are directly related to the web design decisions discussed below. They are not required to understand the engineering concepts in this guide.

item.title: How Loopjacking Hijacks Human Approval in AI Workflows
item.author: OffSec
item.content:encoded: Imagine an AI agent asks you to approve a small payment to a familiar vendor. You check the amount, verify the recipient, and approve it.The workflow continues. A much larger payment goes to a different destination.You return to the approval record. It still contains the original request.This scenario illustrates : a failure in which software uses a human’s approval for one operation to authorize or release something materially different. The experiments discussed here used harmless mock transfers and local recording tools; no money moved.The uncomfortable part is that the human can make the correct decision. The software fails to preserve what that decision authorized.Researcher Adithyan Arun Kumar examines this gap in . The study distinguishes two ways it can happen: an operation changes after approval, or the approval view leaves out consequential details that were present all along. Both break the same expectation: what you approve should be what executes.What a click on “Approve” actually authorizesWhen someone approves a payment, they approve an amount and a recipient. For a file upload, the destination and files matter. For a command, its arguments and execution context can change its consequences.An agent workflow has to carry that meaning through several components. One proposes an action. Another prepares the approval view. The workflow may pause, save its state, and resume later. Eventually, a tool performs the operation.The security requirement extends across that entire path. A record saying “this task was approved” cannot establish that every later action within the task was approved. Even the same tool-call identifier can refer to changed arguments if the implementation permits replacement.For an attacker, that distinction can create an opportunity: influence the operation while retaining someone else’s authorization.A qualifying Loopjacking case therefore requires a genuine approval, a materially different effect outside its scope, and a reachable way for an attacker to make the product consume that approval. The attacker must also lack an equivalent direct route to the effect.When the action changes after approvalState substitution starts with an accurate request. The reviewer sees operation A and approves it. Before execution, attacker-influenced workflow state substitutes operation B, and the system continues using the earlier decision.The study’s Agno AgentOS experiment makes this concrete. Its tested regular-Agent configuration separated two roles: a lower-privileged user could initiate and continue a run, while a distinct administrator could approve the proposed operation.The approved operation was a mock transfer of 20 units to an approved vendor. The operation ultimately dispatched was a mock transfer of 2,000 units to a different destination.The lower-privileged user could neither approve the request nor directly execute the substituted operation. Yet after the administrator approved the original request, the product accepted changed continuation data and dispatched the different transfer. The approval record still described the original operation.In the recorded Agno bundle, this mismatch occurred in five of five trials. Unchanged approved operations executed in five of five controls, while all three direct attempts at the substituted operation were denied. These results apply to the exact tested configuration; they do not measure how frequently deployed systems are affected. The public evidence index documents the boundaries and controls.An additional researcher-built control compared the approved operation with the operation about to execute. It rejected the substitution while allowing the original transfer. That demonstrates a working defense for the tested path, rather than a released Agno fix.When the approval view leaves something outRepresentation mismatch starts with an incomplete view. No change after approval is necessary. The consequential behavior is already encoded in the request, but the approval view does not faithfully represent it.A previously disclosed OpenClaw issue demonstrates this distinction. In the affected command-execution path, approval text could represent only part of a shell command’s execution context. Additional arguments consumed at runtime were absent from that representation.The vendor’s security advisory, which credits the original reporter, describes the mismatch and identifies as the patched release.Kumar’s study reproduced the mismatch on using a harmless temporary marker. The same mismatch was rejected on , while unchanged approved commands continued to work. The approval role was scripted after recording and checking the exact product event: the experiment measured system behavior, not whether people would be deceived by a particular interface. The OpenClaw evidence record preserves that distinction.This explains why freezing a request after approval is an incomplete defense. An immutable request can still be inadequately represented to its reviewer.A control that kept approval intactThe study also included an implementation that preserved the approval boundary. In OpenAI Agents SDK and , ordinary per-call approval remained bound to the invocation across saving and restoring workflow state. Unchanged approved operations executed; changed invocation arguments retaining the call identifier were rejected.For each release, all three unchanged-operation controls passed, and all three mutation trials were rejected without a recorded effect. The negative-control evidence applies to the tested ordinary per-call approval path, not every approval mode or application built around the SDK.That result matters because agent workflows need to pause and resume. Persistence and continuation can coexist with meaningful approval. The implementation has to preserve the operation-specific authorization through those transitions.Where prompt injection fitsPrompt injection can influence what an agent proposes or place attacker-controlled content into a workflow. Loopjacking concerns the subsequent authorization failure: an implementation consumes a human decision for an operation outside its scope. The two can occur together, but Loopjacking does not require prompt injection.Loopjacking groups concrete approval-to-effect failures in agent workflows and distinguishes how they arise. It does not imply that approval integrity is a newly discovered security principle, or that all agent frameworks share one vulnerability.What developers should preserve through executionFor developers, the practical requirement is to make the approval interface and execution system agree on the operation being authorized. Four design choices help make that agreement enforceable:Build the approval view from the operation that will execute. Include the arguments, destination, resources, and context that materially affect the outcome. A readable summary can help, but it cannot replace consequential details.Bind the decision to a protected operation record. Preserve what was approved, who approved it, and the scope and validity of that decision. A task identifier or an “approved” flag is insufficient when the operation underneath it can change.Compare again immediately before execution. Resolve the current operation and check it against the approved record. A material change should stop execution or require fresh approval. Protect the checked operation against further substitution before dispatch.Make approval consumption and audit records precise. Enforce expiry and reuse limits, and record both the approved operation and the operation actually released. Retries should not silently expand what a one-time decision permits.A cryptographic digest can help bind these records, but only if it covers the relevant operation and is protected from tampering. Hashing an incomplete description preserves the same omission.For teams evaluating their own workflows, a useful acceptance test is whether unchanged approved operations succeed while materially different operations require a new decision. The evidence should include the actual effect at the tool boundary; a successful response or an approval entry alone cannot establish that the correct action executed.The study used isolated environments, synthetic identities, and harmless recording tools, with an evidence cutoff of September 10, 2026. It establishes specific implementation failures and working controls. It does not establish ecosystem prevalence, and independent reproduction is not claimed.For a person reviewing an action, approval carries a concrete meaning. The software’s job is to preserve it through execution. An audit trail should show who authorized which operation, and that the operation released stayed within that authorization.

item.title: Cloudflare Keeps 1.1.1.1 Out of Piracy Blocking, Escapes Penalties In France
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: Cloudflare doesn't block pirate sports streaming sites through its 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver in France, only through its CDN. The Paris Judicial Court has now accepted that stance, rejecting [French pay-TV provider] Canal+'s request for penalties of 50,000 euros per site, per day. Interestingly, the court's conclusion relies on statistics provided by Canal+ itself. [...] As a result, Cloudflare will not be penalized under these orders, even though its public DNS resolver is not blocking the sites in question. That is in line with the company's long-standing claim that it doesn't interfere with its DNS.
In its recent transparency reports, Cloudflare repeatedly stated that it hasn't blocked any content through 1.1.1.1, despite orders from French and Italian courts. "To date, Cloudflare has not blocked content through the 1.1.1.1 Public DNS Resolver," the company's latest report reads. [...] Blocking through the CDN is another matter. According to the same report, Cloudflare geoblocked 1,238 domains in France in the second half of 2025, all under a single court order. In the first half of the year, it geoblocked 662 domains under seven orders. Cloudflare recently explained its position to the European Commission, in a submission (PDF) to its Counterfeit and Piracy Watch List consultation, stressing that global public DNS resolvers should not be used to block or restrict access.
Instead, it highlights its real-time pirate stream blocking program, which allows vetted rightsholders to flag pirate streams that run through its network. These streams are disrupted "within seconds," Cloudflare says, without any DNS or IP address blocking. "For live content, where speed is crucial, Cloudflare has built real-time mitigation mechanisms that allow vetted rightsholder partners to flag infringing streams. When those streams are running through our network, we act on them in seconds," Cloudflare informed the Commission. For now, Cloudflare can continue to block pirate sites through its CDN only, while its 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver remains untouched. Canal+ can still appeal the rulings, so it may not be the last we hear of it.

item.title: How David Bratslavsky Is Helping Commercial Real Estate Operators Use AI to Win Deals
item.author: Sanya Kapoor
item.content:encoded: Multifamily sales volume reached $22.8 billion in the first quarter of 2026. Deal velocity is climbing. Capital is moving. And at most investment firms, the bottleneck is not sourcing or financing. It is the hours an acquisitions team spends transferring numbers from rent rolls and operating statements into Excel before anyone can run a single projection. built QuickData.ai to eliminate that transfer step. The platform is an Excel add-in that reads multifamily financial documents and places the extracted data directly into whatever underwriting model the firm already uses. The company reports 99.3% accuracy on rent-roll extraction and identification rate for trailing twelve-month operating statement line items. More than 800 multifamily professionals use the tool, according to the company, at $99 per user per month.That product was the starting point. What followed was a consulting practice that now helps commercial real estate firms build AI capabilities across their operations.A Speed Problem With a Dollar ValueFor a multifamily investor evaluating twenty or thirty acquisition opportunities per month, underwriting speed has a direct relationship to deal flow coverage. Every property requires the same preparation: pull the rent roll data, categorize the T12 expenses, normalize the offering memorandum figures, and populate the firm's financial model. The mechanical portion of that work, the part that involves reading a PDF and typing numbers into cells, accounts for the majority of the time an analyst spends before the actual evaluation begins."QuickData helps multifamily professionals underwrite deals 10x faster by automating rent roll, T12, and OM data entry into Excel," said David Bratslavsky, founder of QuickData.ai, describing the product's core function.Users save an average of 15 hours per month, according to QuickData.ai. For a three-person acquisitions team, that represents 45 hours redirected from data entry to deal evaluation. In a market where the firm that completes its underwriting first is often the firm that controls the negotiation, those hours carry a measurable cost when wasted and a measurable advantage when recovered.The tool was trained specifically on multifamily document formats, according to the company, which is why generic document-processing software tends to produce unreliable results in this sector. A rent roll from one property management company categorises charges differently than one from another. T12 line items vary by operator. Offering memorandums follows no standard layout. The extraction engine was built to handle those inconsistencies rather than guess through them.Working with investment firms on the underwriting problem, Bratslavsky saw that rent-roll extraction was one instance of a pattern that repeated across the entire business. Leasing teams read lease amendments to track critical dates. Asset managers compile monthly reports to explain budget variances. Investor relations teams turn portfolio data into quarterly updates. Each of these tasks involves finding, organising, checking, and moving information from one place to another.That recognition led Bratslavsky to build a consulting practice around what he describes as AI skills: reusable sets of instructions, trained on a firm's own documents and terminology, that handle specific repetitive tasks. One skill might categorize operating expenses. Another might reconcile conflicting figures across documents. A third might populate a quarterly investor report from reviewed data.The consulting engagements follow a consistent structure. Bratslavsky works with the firm's employees to identify a task, document how it currently works, build an AI skill that replicates it, and test the output against real documents. The employees learn the process so they can maintain and extend the automations after the engagement ends.The practice now works with multifamily, office, and industrial firms, brokers, and lenders, applying the same method to lease abstraction, asset management reporting, and covenant monitoring. Bratslavsky, who has worked as a fractional chief technology officer, brings a background that combines technology operations with real estate investing.The investor who evaluates forty opportunities per month and the investor who evaluates fifteen are not equally positioned, even if their judgment is identical. The difference is coverage. When underwriting preparation takes less time, more properties get a full evaluation instead of a preliminary screen and a pass.QuickData.ai addresses the mechanical layer of that preparation. The consulting practice addresses the organisational layer: teaching firms to apply AI to the other repetitive tasks that accumulate across acquisitions, asset management, and investor reporting. Together, they represent Bratslavsky's answer to a question that most multifamily firms are asking in some form: how do you increase deal coverage without proportionally increasing headcount?The answer, in his framing, is not to replace the people doing the work. It is to remove the hours they spend on tasks that do not require their expertise, and let them apply that time to the decisions that do.

item.title: The Lawyer Who's Building His Own Version Of Legal AI
item.author: Sanya Kapoor
item.content:encoded: Daman Singh Saduara didn't set out to compete with Westlaw. He set out to be a lawyer.Saduara trained in law at the University of Leicester, completed an LLM at the University of Miami, and interned with Aliette Rodriguez's team at Shutts & Bowen in Miami, one of the country's largest firms. Everything about that path pointed toward a bar exam and a career inside a major legal practice. He chose not to sit the exam. Instead, he built , an AI automation and consulting company, in Miami in January 2026, with his brother, Gurvir Singh Saduara, as co-founder. Gurvir studied mechanical engineering and 3D robotics at Conestoga College in Kitchener-Waterloo, a technical background that now feeds directly into how the two of them approach product development.Now Saduara is turning that same instinct toward an industry he knows from the inside: legal services.What law school actually taught him"Everything I learned in law, I'm using now," Saduara said. "I just don't have to ask permission to build with it." For a founder without a computer science background, that's not a throwaway line. It's the whole thesis behind everything he's built since.Saduara credits Marike Paulson, one of his professors, with pushing him to publish early in his academic career, an exercise he says forced him to think clearly in writing before he ever tried explaining an idea out loud. Howard Kwon taught him how to integrate AI into daily workflows inside an actual law firm setting, which turned out to be a preview of exactly the kind of problem Saduara is now trying to solve at scale, years before he had a company to apply it to. A separate memory stuck just as hard. Daniel Gonzalez and Mark Cheskin, partners at Hogan Lovells in Miami, once mentioned in passing a former student who'd gone on to become a client of their own firm. Saduara says it completely reframed how he thought about ambition. The goal was never just landing a job at a top firm. It was becoming the kind of person a top firm would want as a client.That reframing is now the business plan, aimed at an entire industry rather than a single career.Two products, one very specific problemSaduara's newest venture is , an AI company he owns that builds tools spanning websites, ad campaigns across Meta, Snapchat, LinkedIn, and X, and AI-generated content for companies and brands that want a presence without a full production team. Its first two products both target the legal industry directly, and they're built to solve different versions of the same underlying problem: every law firm works differently, and most existing tools don't account for that.Hawk is a plug-and-play legal research and writing tool, positioned as a direct alternative to Westlaw and LexisNexis. Saduara describes it in blunt terms: purchase it, plug it into your existing workflow, done. No custom integration, no months-long onboarding process, no retraining an entire department on a new system. It's built for firms that want the capability without the operational lift.Hawk 2.0 takes the opposite approach. It's a fully white-label, enterprise-level platform built specifically for law firms that want to shape the tool around themselves rather than adapt to someone else's design. Name, automation logic, feature set, even the interface, all of it is customizable. Where Hawk is meant to slot into a firm's existing process without disruption, Hawk 2.0 is meant to eventually become the firm's process."Every law firm does legal research and legal writing differently," Saduara said. "Most tools ask firms to adapt to one fixed system. We're building the opposite, something that adapts to them."Betting on the firms that already know what good looks likeSaduara isn't planning a wide public launch out of the gate, and he's direct about why. He wants Hawk tested first at the University of Leicester and the University of Miami, the two schools where he studied, with trials aimed specifically at finding bugs and stress-testing the tool in a real academic legal environment before it goes anywhere near a paying client. It's a deliberate choice to start with institutions he trusts and that already operate to rigorous standards, rather than opening access broadly and hoping the product holds up under pressure.Hawk 2.0 is targeted for an early 2027 release, with the base Hawk platform following in mid to late 2027. The sequencing reflects how Saduara is thinking about risk. Enterprise clients working directly with his team on a customized build can absorb early iteration in a way a self-serve product can't, so the more controlled release comes first, and the plug-and-play version follows once the underlying system has been tested against real firm demands.Both his own credibility and Loophole's are staked on the tool working the way it's supposed to from day one, not on being first to market. "I'm not building this because I left law behind," Saduara said. "I'm building it because I didn't."For a founder who walked away from a conventional legal career specifically to avoid being boxed into one way of operating, building a legal AI platform designed around flexibility isn't ironic. It's the same instinct, aimed at a different industry, built on the same conviction that no two law firms or careers should have to fit the same mold.

This is a simplified guide to an AI model called Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 maintained by Qwen. If you like these kinds of analysis, join AIModels.fyi or follow us on Twitter.

Model overview

Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 is an enhanced image editing model from Qwen that builds on its predecessor with improvements in consistency and capability. This model handles image-to-image transformations through text prompts, allowing users to edit and manipulate images in sophisticated ways. The improvements in this version focus on reducing image drift, enhancing character consistency, and integrating community-created LoRA capabilities. Compared to related models like Qwen-Image-Edit-Plus, this version places special emphasis on practical industrial applications and geometric reasoning.

Model inputs and outputs

The model accepts images and text prompts to generate edited versions of those images. Users provide reference images along with detailed instructions about desired modifications, and the model outputs new images reflecting those changes while maintaining visual consistency and quality.

Inputs

  • Images: One or multiple input images to be edited or used as reference material
  • Prompt: Text description of the desired edits or transformations
  • Configuration parameters: Settings like guidance scale, inference steps, and seed values to control generation behavior

Outputs

  • Edited images: Generated images reflecting the requested modifications while preserving important visual characteristics from the input

Capabilities

The model handles character consistency across edits, preserving identity and visual traits when making imaginative changes to portraits. It can fuse multiple person images into coherent group photos while maintaining consistency across all subjects. The model includes built-in support for popular community LoRAs, enabling effects like realistic lighting control and multi-angle viewpoint generation without additional tuning. For industrial applications, it performs batch product design variations and material replacement on components. The model demonstrates enhanced geometric reasoning, capable of generating construction lines and annotations for design purposes.

What can I use it for?

Creative professionals can use this for portrait editing that maintains character identity while exploring different styles and contexts. Fashion and product designers benefit from batch generation of design variations and material swaps for industrial components. The model works for creative composition tasks, enabling the combination of separate person images into unified group photographs. Teams working on industrial design can generate multiple product iterations and explore material alternatives efficiently. Content creators can perform complex edits that require both semantic understanding and visual consistency, from fantasy character transformations to realistic lighting adjustments. Explore related research on intelligent interactive image editing systems for additional context on this capability space.

Things to try

Experiment with portrait editing by providing a photo and describing a different context or styling while watching the model preserve facial features and identity. Test multi-person editing by uploading two separate portraits and requesting them to appear together in a specific scene. Try leveraging the integrated LoRA capabilities to add professional lighting effects without needing to load additional models. For industrial workflows, batch generate product design variations by making iterative edits with different material descriptions. Explore geometric reasoning by requesting the model add construction lines or guides to images for design annotation purposes. Investigate the difference between single-subject and multi-person consistency by comparing results on individual versus group photos.
