If you like these kinds of analysis, join AIModels.fyi [https://www.aimodels.fyi/?utm_source=hackernoon&utm_medium=referral] or follow us on Twitter [https://x.com/aimodelsfyi].THE CURSE OF RESOLUTION IN PHYSICS SIMULATIONSImagine watching water flow through sand at two different zoom levels. At low zoom, you see the overall current pushing through the domain. At high zoom, individual sand grains create turbulence and complex flow patterns that wouldn't be visible from far away. To capture both, you need the high-zoom video, which takes forever to compute. Yet you can't simply use the low-zoom version because those tiny grain-scale interactions fundamentally change how the bulk flow behaves.This is the core tension in finite element methods, the standard tool scientists use to approximate solutions to the differential equations governing physical systems. In these methods, computational cost scales brutally with resolution. Double your resolution in two dimensions and you create 16 times more elements. In three dimensions, that's 64 times more. This isn't a problem you solve by throwing more compute at it indefinitely. High-resolution simulations are accurate but prohibitively expensive. Coarse simulations are fast but miss crucial small-scale details that ripple through the big picture.The multiscale structures in physics aren't incidental; they're fundamental. Small-scale heterogeneity in materials, turbulent fluctuations in fluids, grain-boundary effects in crystals, all these phenomena affect macroscopic behavior in ways that can't simply be averaged away. Yet capturing them requires the computational horsepower of a high-resolution simulation, creating a genuine impasse between speed and accuracy.WHY TRADITIONAL MULTISCALE METHODS DON'T QUITE SOLVE ITResearchers have known for decades that you need something smarter than brute-force high-resolution simulation. The traditional approach looks like dividing a puzzle into pieces. You solve the problem at a coarse scale, figure out how that coarse solution influences the fine scale, then solve the fine-scale problem in each region, coupling the results back together. Mathematically, this works. Computationally, it's more involved than it sounds.Methods like homogenization and multiscale finite element methods are mathematically rigorous and can provide guarantees about their approximations. But they require solving auxiliary problems, like the "cell problems" in homogenization theory, to understand how fine scales feed back into coarse scales. For complex materials or irregular geometries, these auxiliary problems can be nearly as expensive as the original simulation. You're trading one hard problem for several smaller hard problems, which is an improvement but not revolutionary.The core limitation is that multiscale methods still require explicit computation of fine-scale corrections. You don't truly escape the resolution curse; you just distribute the work differently. For time-dependent problems or when you need to run many similar simulations, this overhead becomes prohibitive.SUPER-RESOLUTION AS LEARNED MULTISCALE CORRECTIONWhat if you bypassed mathematical derivation entirely and instead let a neural network learn the relationship between coarse and fine scales from examples? You run many simulations at both coarse and fine resolution, showing the network thousands of pairs, and ask it to learn the underlying pattern. Then, for new problems, you run only the cheap coarse simulation and let the network fill in the fine details.This reframes the multiscale problem fundamentally. Instead of asking "how do I mathematically derive the fine-scale correction from the coarse solution," you ask "what statistical relationship exists between coarse-resolution snapshots of physics and fine-resolution snapshots?" Train a network to learn that relationship, and it becomes a reusable tool.The brilliant insight is that you don't need to hand-derive the multiscale coupling. You're leveraging an assumption about the physical world: that small-scale structures follow patterns that are learnable and repeatable across different scenarios. If those patterns truly reflect the underlying physics, the network should generalize beyond its training distribution. It should work on upsampling factors it never saw, on material properties it never explicitly trained on.Continuous super-resolution bridges coarse and fine scales. The orange region shows in-distribution scenarios (upsampling factors up to 16x), while the blue region shows out-of-distribution tests where the method extrapolates to 32x and beyond. The orange region shows in-distribution scenarios (upsampling factors up to 16x), while the blue region shows out-of-distribution tests where the method extrapolates to 32x and beyond.This is where the paper departs from typical deep learning applications. It's not just applying image super-resolution to scientific data. It's asking whether neural networks can learn and extrapolate the structure of multiscale physics.THE ARCHITECTURE: LOCAL IMPLICIT TRANSFORMERS LEARN ACROSS SCALESBuilding a network that handles both coarse context and fine reconstruction simultaneously requires solving a specific technical challenge. How do you make a neural network that respects multiscale structure, preserves both large-scale features and fine details, and works at arbitrary query locations, not just fixed grid points?The answer involves two key components working in concert. First, local implicit neural representations (LIIF) treat space as continuous rather than discrete. Instead of the network learning a grid of pixel values, it learns a continuous function that can predict the field value at any spatial coordinate, like x=0.1234, y=0.5678. The coarse module processes the coarse finite element solution and extracts features. The fine module takes those features plus a query coordinate and outputs the fine-resolution prediction at that specific location.Second, a transformer architecture handles the multiscale learning. Transformers excel at learning long-range dependencies and attention patterns, which maps directly to the physics: the fine-scale behavior at one location depends on coarse features potentially across a large region. The transformer learns which parts of the coarse domain matter for predicting details at any given location.The architecture processes coarse finite element data through feature extraction, then uses a local implicit function in the transformer to predict fine-scale corrections at arbitrary spatial coordinates. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/network_v2.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/network_v2.jpg] The architecture processes coarse finite element data through feature extraction, then uses a local implicit function in the transformer to predict fine-scale corrections at arbitrary spatial coordinates.The elegance of this design is that it separates the two jobs cleanly. The coarse module sees the big picture. The fine module handles spatial interpolation and detail generation. The transformer connects them by learning which coarse features to attend to for each fine-scale prediction.THE FREQUENCY PROBLEM: WHY GABOR WAVELETS FIX NEURAL NETWORK BLINDNESSHere's a subtle but critical problem that most practitioners would miss. Neural networks are biased learners. When you show them spatial data and ask them to predict values, they naturally learn smooth, low-frequency features first. Their internal "perception" gravitates toward blurry versions of the input. For multiscale corrections, this is backwards. You desperately need the network to pay serious attention to high-frequency details that create the fine structure.This isn't a failure of the network; it's a feature of how they learn. Low-frequency functions are often the "easy" solution that reduces loss quickly and smoothly. Standard positional encodings help somewhat, but the paper proposes something more targeted: Gabor wavelets as coordinate encodings.Gabor functions are sinusoidal waves modulated by a Gaussian envelope, and they're particularly good at capturing localized frequency structure. By encoding the spatial coordinates using Gabor wavelets instead of simple sinusoids, the network gets a built-in curriculum that encourages it to respect fine-scale structure from the start. It's like giving the network glasses that make high-frequency details visually prominent.The impact is visible in frequency-space analysis. Using radial power spectral density (RAPSD), you can decompose how much energy the predicted field contains at each frequency scale.Frequency analysis via radial power spectral density (RAPSD) shows that the proposed method preserves high-frequency content that simpler approaches lose, matching the ground truth spectrum more closely. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/rapsd_compare.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/rapsd_compare.jpg] Frequency analysis via radial power spectral density (RAPSD) shows that the proposed method preserves high-frequency content that simpler approaches lose, matching the ground truth spectrum more closely.The proposed method maintains the correct frequency spectrum. Competitors without this frequency-aware encoding produce outputs that are systematically too smooth, missing the sharp transitions and fine textures that characterize physical fields.COMPARING PATCHES INSTEAD OF PIXELS: STOCHASTIC COSINE SIMILARITYIf you want a neural network to produce physically realistic fine details, you can't just compare its prediction to ground truth pixel-by-pixel. A pixel-level loss function like mean squared error will push the network toward a blurry average of many possible fine structures, which looks wrong to human eyes and doesn't capture the structural patterns of real physical fields. The paper recognizes that "perception is often preferred over distortion," meaning scientists care whether the fine-scale pattern looks and behaves like real physics, not just whether numbers match exactly.The solution is stochastic cosine similarity (SCS), which compares local regions (patches) rather than individual points. Instead of asking "does prediction[pixel i] match ground_truth[pixel i]?", it asks "does the pattern of features in prediction[region j] match the pattern in ground_truth[region j]?" Cosine similarity measures how aligned two vectors are in direction, ignoring their magnitude. This encourages the network to get the structure right even if it's shifted slightly or scaled differently. Stochastic means you sample random patches during training, giving the network diverse supervision across the domain.Training curves show that incorporating stochastic cosine similarity loss improves convergence and final reconstruction quality compared to standard pixel-level losses. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/loss_curve.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/loss_curve.jpg] Training curves show that incorporating stochastic cosine similarity loss improves convergence and final reconstruction quality compared to standard pixel-level losses.This is a subtle but important detail that bridges the gap between mathematical accuracy and visual/structural fidelity. A network optimized only for pixel-level MSE will produce outputs that look blurry but have low numerical error. A network optimized with SCS learns to preserve the local structure and patterns that make the field look physically plausible to human inspection and domain-expert evaluation.IN-DISTRIBUTION VERSUS OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION: HOW FAR CAN THE PATTERN GENERALIZEThere's a critical question hidden in every learning-based approach to scientific computing: how much can the network actually generalize? If you train on simulations with upsampling factor up to 16x, can it handle 32x? If you train on one type of material coefficient, can it work on completely different physical scenarios?The distinction matters enormously. Any neural network can memorize training data. The real test of whether you've learned a physics-driven pattern, rather than just captured statistical artifacts of your training set, is whether it works on new configurations and extrapolation scenarios.The experiments are structured to test both regimes carefully. The network trains on coarse-fine pairs with upsampling factors up to 16x. Then it's tested on 32x upsampling it never saw during training, as well as scenarios with different material properties represented by different coefficient maps. This tests not just the model's capacity to interpolate, but its ability to extrapolate the learned multiscale patterns.Visual comparison shows the method handles both in-distribution cases (left, upsampling factor 16x) and out-of-distribution extrapolation (right, upsampling factor 32x). The reconstructed field structure remains recognizable even beyond the training regime. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/sota_mix.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/sota_mix.jpg] Visual comparison shows the method handles both in-distribution cases (left, upsampling factor 16x) and out-of-distribution extrapolation (right, upsampling factor 32x). The reconstructed field structure remains recognizable even beyond the training regime.The results show the method generalizes reasonably well out-of-distribution, though with some expected degradation as you push further from the training regime. This is the critical finding because it justifies calling this a "learned multiscale correction strategy" rather than just image super-resolution applied to finite element data. The network has learned something about how multiscale structure works in general, not just memorized specific examples.To understand how the network adapts across different physical scenarios, the approach includes conditioning on material properties. By feeding different coefficient maps to the encoder, the network learns to adjust its multiscale correction strategy based on the physical parameters.Conditional super-resolution demonstrates that the model adapts its correction pattern based on different coefficient maps and upsampling factors, showing learned flexibility across physical scenarios. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/condition.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/condition.jpg] Conditional super-resolution demonstrates that the model adapts its correction pattern based on different coefficient maps and upsampling factors, showing learned flexibility across physical scenarios.The network learns that different materials and heterogeneities require different fine-scale correction patterns, and it captures this adaptability in its weights.WHAT THE NUMBERS ACTUALLY TELL USAt the end, you need empirical validation: is this actually better than alternatives? How much better? The paper compares against other super-resolution methods, other learning approaches like basic neural networks and other implicit neural representation variants, and standard finite element upsampling baselines.The comparison metrics matter enormously because, as noted earlier, pixel-level error doesn't capture what scientists actually care about. The paper includes both traditional metrics (mean squared error, mean absolute error) and perceptual metrics that measure whether the fine-scale structure aligns with ground truth.Sliced pixel comparisons show the proposed method follows sharp transitions and fine details more closely than competitors, especially at boundaries and high-frequency regions. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/sliced_compare_v3.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/sliced_compare_v3.jpg] Sliced pixel comparisons show the proposed method follows sharp transitions and fine details more closely than competitors, especially at boundaries and high-frequency regions.When you slice specific pixel sequences and compare methods, the proposed approach tracks the ground truth more faithfully than alternatives. Competitors either miss sharp transitions entirely or smear them out, while this method preserves fine structure with fidelity.Residual visualizations reveal where the improvements are largest.Residual differences between the proposed method and simpler local implicit transformer baselines show that gains are concentrated in high-frequency regions and sharp transitions. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/csr.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/csr.jpg] Residual differences between the proposed method and simpler local implicit transformer baselines show that gains are concentrated in high-frequency regions and sharp transitions.The visualization multiplies residuals by 20 times for visibility, but the pattern is clear: the proposed method reduces errors especially where fine structure matters most, at boundaries and transitions between regions with different properties.The paper also tests the method on real-world soil pattern data, demonstrating that the learned patterns transfer to actual scientific data beyond the synthetic training regime.Real-world soil patterns show that the method generalizes to natural spatial heterogeneity, successfully reconstructing fine-scale structure from coarse observations. [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/real_world.jpg] [https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07576/real_world.jpg] Real-world soil patterns show that the method generalizes to natural spatial heterogeneity, successfully reconstructing fine-scale structure from coarse observations.This connection to real data is important because it grounds the work in practical utility. The method isn't just clever on carefully-curated synthetic examples; it works on the types of data scientists actually encounter.WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE NUMBERSThe paper ultimately succeeds because it solves a three-part problem elegantly. First, it reframes multiscale simulation as a learned-pattern problem, replacing hand-derived mathematical relationships with neural network induction from examples. Second, it builds neural network architecture specifically designed for multiscale structure: local implicit representations for continuous spatial prediction, transformers to learn long-range dependencies, and Gabor wavelets to overcome the frequency bias in neural networks. Third, it uses perceptual supervision via stochastic cosine similarity to ensure the learned patterns are physically meaningful, not just mathematically smooth.The individual components are solid engineering. But their combination creates something genuinely useful: a system that learns a generalizable multiscale correction that works even on unseen scenarios, generating high-frequency details that reflect actual physics rather than neural network artifacts.For scientists and engineers, this offers a practical advantage. Run expensive multiscale simulations once to train a network. Then use that network to quickly augment fast coarse simulations with plausible fine-scale structure. It's not a replacement for rigorous multiscale mathematics, but it's a powerful complement, trading theoretical guarantees for computational speed and practical effectiveness. Model overview

ltx-2-19b/distilled/extend-video is a specialized tool from fal-ai designed to extend videos by generating synchronized audio. This distilled version of LTX-2 provides a streamlined approach to video-to-audio generation. If you need to extend video content with different model versions, alternatives like ltxv-13b-098-distilled/extend and ltx-video-13b-distilled/extend offer different architectural approaches to the same task.

Capabilities

This model generates audio that matches existing video content, allowing creators to add synchronized soundtracks to silent or partially dubbed videos. The distilled nature means it processes requests with reduced computational overhead compared to full-scale versions, making it practical for production workflows. The audio generation adapts to the visual content, ensuring temporal alignment and coherence with on-screen events and scene transitions.

What can I use it for?

Content creators can use this model to add professional audio layers to silent footage, completing video projects that lack proper sound design or dialogue. Educational institutions might enhance instructional videos with narration. Marketing teams can extend raw video captures with branded audio elements. The distilled version makes these applications accessible without requiring extensive hardware resources. Understanding how this fits into broader audio synthesis approaches can benefit from research into long-form video-to-audio generation techniques.

Things to try

Start by testing with simple videos where the visual narrative is clear and straightforward, as the model will generate audio that corresponds to those visual cues. Experiment with different video lengths to understand the model's optimal range for audio generation. Try feeding it videos with distinct visual moments or scene changes to see how the audio responds to those transitions. Compare the generated audio quality against your original footage to identify where the model excels and where manual adjustments might enhance results.

This is a simplified guide to an AI model called GLM-Image maintained by zai-org. If you like these kinds of analysis, join AIModels.fyi or follow us on Twitter.

Model overview

GLM-Image combines an autoregressive generator with a diffusion decoder to create images from text and perform sophisticated image editing tasks. The 9B autoregressive component generates a compact visual token sequence, which the 7B diffusion decoder then expands into high-resolution outputs. This hybrid architecture delivers competitive image quality while excelling in scenarios demanding precise text rendering and knowledge-intensive details. Unlike pure diffusion models that struggle with text accuracy, this approach handles complex information expression with greater fidelity. The model maintains the semantic understanding capabilities of GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking while specializing in visual generation rather than multimodal reasoning.

Model inputs and outputs

GLM-Image processes both textual prompts and image inputs to generate or modify visual content. The system accepts text descriptions of arbitrary length and complexity, along with optional reference images for conditional generation tasks. The model outputs high-resolution images ranging from 1024x1024 to 2048x1024 pixels, maintaining visual coherence and detail quality across diverse generation scenarios.

Inputs

  • Text prompts describing desired image content, including detailed specifications for layout, composition, and visual elements
  • Reference images for image-to-image tasks such as editing and style transfer
  • Multiple reference images for maintaining consistency across subjects in multi-image generation scenarios
  • Guidance parameters controlling the strength of prompt adherence and generation diversity

Outputs

  • Generated images in PNG format at specified dimensions
  • High-fidelity visual content with accurate text rendering and fine-grained details
  • Edited or transformed images preserving identity and compositional elements from source images

Capabilities

The model generates images from text descriptions with particular strength in information-dense layouts. Recipe illustrations with ingredient lists, numbered steps, and visual hierarchies render with precise text and accurate proportions. Image-to-image capabilities include background replacement, style transfer between images, identity-preserving generation for people and objects, and multi-subject consistency maintenance. The decoupled reinforcement learning training using the GRPO algorithm enhances both semantic alignment and visual detail quality, with the autoregressive module improving aesthetic understanding and the diffusion decoder refining texture fidelity and text accuracy. Post-training feedback signals target low-frequency features like composition and high-frequency elements like texture, creating nuanced control over output characteristics.

What can I use it for?

Design professionals can generate detailed marketing materials with embedded text and complex layouts without manual typography adjustments. Educational content creators produce recipe cards, instructional guides, and infographics with embedded text that renders correctly on the first attempt. E-commerce businesses create product photography variations with consistent branding and identity. Visual artists explore style transfer to apply artistic treatments while preserving subject identity. Publishers generate magazine layouts and illustrated guides combining dense information with high visual quality. The model's accuracy with text-based content opens applications previously requiring manual post-processing or graphic design expertise. Compare this capability to Z-Image-Turbo for efficiency-focused workflows or visualglm-6b for combined understanding and generation tasks.

Things to try

Test the model's text rendering accuracy with prompts containing typography-heavy content like posters, menus, or certificates. Generate illustrated recipes or instructional manuals with step-by-step visual guides and embedded text descriptions. Perform background replacement while preserving foreground subjects, then compare results when providing multiple reference images for consistency constraints. Apply artistic styles to photographs while maintaining face identity for personal portrait variations. Create magazine-style layouts with multiple content sections, experimenting with guidance scale values to balance creative interpretation against strict prompt adherence. The Glyph Encoder text module distinguishes this model from standard diffusion approaches, making typography-intensive generation a particularly revealing test case.

This is a simplified guide to an AI model called IQuest-Coder-V1-40B-Loop-Instruct maintained by IQuestLab. If you like these kinds of analysis, join AIModels.fyi or follow us on Twitter.

Model overview

IQuest-Coder-V1-40B-Loop-Instruct represents a specialized variant of the IQuest-Coder-V1 family, a collection of code language models built by IQuestLab for advanced software engineering tasks. This 40 billion parameter model uses a recurrent transformer design that processes information through two iterations, allowing it to balance model capacity with practical deployment requirements. The Loop variant achieves competitive performance on major coding benchmarks including SWE-Bench Verified (81.4%), BigCodeBench (49.9%), and LiveCodeBench v6 (81.1%), placing it alongside other leading code models like the standard 40B Instruct variant.

Model inputs and outputs

The model accepts natural language instructions and code-related prompts, processing them through its 128K token context window to generate coherent code solutions and explanations. It produces code snippets, complete implementations, debugging assistance, and technical explanations based on user queries.

Inputs

  • Natural language instructions: Requests for code generation, refactoring, or debugging
  • Code snippets: Partial implementations to complete or improve
  • Programming problems: Tasks requiring algorithmic solutions
  • Chat messages: Multi-turn conversations formatted for instruction-following

Outputs

  • Generated code: Complete, working implementations in multiple programming languages
  • Code explanations: Detailed breakdowns of logic and functionality
  • Debugging suggestions: Fixes for errors and optimization recommendations
  • Technical documentation: Comments and explanations embedded in generated code

Capabilities

The model handles complex coding scenarios through its code-flow training approach, which learns from repository evolution patterns and real-world development workflows rather than treating code as static text. It supports up to 128K tokens natively, enabling it to work with entire files, multiple related modules, or detailed project context without requiring additional scaling techniques. The Loop mechanism allows the model to refine its outputs iteratively, improving solution quality within a single generation pass.

Temperature settings of 0.6, TopP of 0.85, and TopK of 20 are recommended for optimal performance. The model demonstrates strong reasoning capabilities for competitive programming problems, tool usage in agentic software engineering scenarios, and general-purpose coding assistance tasks.

What can I use it for?

Organizations can deploy this model for autonomous code generation pipelines, reducing development time on routine implementation tasks. Software engineering teams can use it as a pair programming assistant that understands repository-scale context, helping developers navigate unfamiliar codebases or generate boilerplate code. The model serves well in educational settings where students need immediate feedback on coding exercises, or in enterprise environments building internal coding assistants. Companies building developer tools can integrate it via the vLLM framework to create OpenAI-compatible APIs, monetizing through usage-based pricing or subscription tiers.

Things to try

Experiment with providing the model large code repositories or entire project directories within the 128K context window to see how effectively it understands interconnected code relationships and generates implementations that maintain consistency across multiple files. Test its performance on complex refactoring tasks where understanding the broader codebase matters more than isolated code generation. Try using it iteratively within a single conversation to progressively improve and debug implementations, leveraging its instruction-following design for multi-step problem solving. Compare its outputs against the standard Instruct variant to understand the practical differences the Loop mechanism introduces in solution quality versus generation speed.

This is a simplified guide to an AI model called HyperCLOVAX-SEED-Think-32B maintained by naver-hyperclovax. If you like these kinds of analysis, join AIModels.fyi or follow us on Twitter.

Model overview

HyperCLOVAX-SEED-Think-32B is a text-to-text language model developed by naver-hyperclovax that combines advanced reasoning capabilities with efficient model design. This model represents part of NAVER's effort to create high-performance language models without simply scaling up parameter counts. The Think series focuses on enhancing reasoning abilities through specialized training techniques. Similar models in this family include the HyperCLOVAX-SEED-Think-14B, which uses pruning and knowledge distillation techniques, as well as text-focused alternatives like the HyperCLOVAX-SEED-Text-Instruct-1.5B for lighter-weight applications.

Model inputs and outputs

The model processes text input and generates text output, making it suitable for conversational tasks, reasoning-heavy problems, and text generation applications. With 32 billion parameters, it handles complex linguistic patterns and multi-step reasoning tasks that require deeper computational capacity.

Inputs

  • Text prompts of varying lengths and complexity
  • Instructions for specific tasks or reasoning problems
  • Context for understanding user intent and domain-specific knowledge

Outputs

  • Generated text responding to input prompts
  • Reasoning chains that show intermediate steps for complex problems
  • Structured responses formatted according to task requirements

Capabilities

This model handles sophisticated text understanding and generation tasks with particular strength in reasoning-heavy applications. It can tackle multi-step problem solving, provide detailed explanations, engage in extended conversations, and process complex instructions. The architecture emphasizes both reasoning quality and computational efficiency, enabling practical deployment across various scenarios without requiring the largest possible models.

What can I use it for?

The model serves well for applications requiring deep reasoning, such as question answering on complex topics, technical content generation, code explanation and debugging assistance, and educational tutoring. Companies can leverage this model for customer support systems that need to handle intricate queries, content creation platforms requiring nuanced writing, and research applications where reasoning transparency matters. The efficient design makes it viable for integration into products where computational resources are limited compared to larger alternatives.

Things to try

Experiment with prompts that explicitly ask for step-by-step reasoning or chain-of-thought explanations to unlock the full potential of the reasoning capabilities. Test how well it handles domain-specific problems by providing relevant context in your prompts. Compare its performance against simpler models on tasks requiring multiple reasoning steps to understand where the additional parameters provide measurable benefit. Try adjusting the detail level of your instructions to see how it responds to both minimal and comprehensive guidance.

item.title: Meta Doesn't Need to Win the AI Race: It Already Owns the Starting Grid
item.author: Benny Doda
item.content:encoded: Muse looks like another AI agent on the surface. When you look closer, you realise it’s a much bigger bet they are making. They are assuming the real prize in AI isn't the smartest model, but the system that knows who you are, understands what you want, and has permission to act on your behalf.The easiest way to misunderstand Meta's new Muse agent is to treat it as another entrant in the increasingly ridiculous AI model horse race.OpenAI releases their something-or-other, Anthropic responds, and then Google moves. A benchmark changes and Reddit declares somebody dead, and then X spends 48 hours announcing that one company has achieved AGI and another has become completely irrelevant and we are all cooked. Short race finished, and then everybody moves onto the next race.Against that background, Muse seemed to arrive rather suddenly. Meta launched it on September 8, and within days it had climbed to the top of the US App Store. Reuters reported 2.8 million downloads in its first 12 days. Muse can manage emails, research purchases, book travel, use financial information, complete transactions, and continue working after you have closed the app. Automation invasion for the normies has finally arrived.It looked like Zuckerberg had suddenly turned up at the agent party, but if you have been watching closely, he hadn't.Meta founded its Fundamental AI Research operation in 2013. Meta AI was already embedded inside Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger at scale by the time 2024 finally rolled around. In April 2025, the company launched a standalone Meta AI app specifically designed to remember context and personalise itself using information people had already chosen to share across Meta products. By May that year, Zuckerberg said Meta AI had reached one billion monthly users; how they count that is very interesting. Later in 2025, Meta announced that interactions with its AI products would become another signal used to personalise content and advertising across connected Meta accounts. This is 4D chess right here.Then came Muse Spark, Meta's new model family, followed by agentic capabilities that connected Meta AI to email and calendars and allowed it to make plans and complete work. Muse is not the beginning of that story; it’s just the thing that makes you take notice when they deemed it was the right time. I think a lot of the AI industry is still looking at the wrong scoreboard.The model race matters. It just might not matter as much as we think.For the one percent of users who spend their lives switching between Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, Grok, Kimi, and whatever was released last Thursday, model performance matters enormously. They notice a five-point coding improvement; they change subscriptions because an agent suddenly became better at spreadsheets. Most of the planet doesn’t behave like this; they are the exception.’Meta's Family of Apps averaged 3.6 billion daily users in June. In the second quarter of 2026, the company generated $60.8 billion in revenue, of which $59.36 billion came from advertising. That means roughly 97.6% of Meta's quarterly revenue still came from ads. I recently wrote about Amazon banning access to agents on its platform. It fundamentally ruins the platform economics for Amazon, as they do $68 billion a year in advertising revenue, approximately 9.57% of their total revenue.That matters because Meta has spent twenty years becoming extraordinarily good at one particular problem: understanding what gets us human beings to look at something, click something, share something, buy something, or come back tomorrow. AI is now making that machine better.Meta told investors that Instagram time spent grew by double digits year-on-year in the second quarter, largely because of improvements in ‘Feed and Reels’ recommendations. Facebook video time increased 9% globally. Meta says its newer recommendation architecture draws on deeper user history, while its LLMs increasingly analyse content, interests and past interactions to improve predictions about what individual users will care about next.Zuckerberg was explicit about the advantage during Meta's earnings call. He described Meta as a company that builds consumer products reaching billions of people and, once something works, knows how to scale it to an enormous audience.That may be the part of the AI race Silicon Valley keeps underestimating, and why I think Meta could still be hugely underrated as a stock, because the best model can win a benchmark, but distribution wins Tuesday morning.Muse doesn't just want prompts. It needs context.For a personal agent to actually be useful, it can’t know only what you typed into a chatbot yesterday. It needs to know your calendar, your email, what you bought, where you need to be, what your partner told you, which flight you booked, what you can afford, which people matter to you, and which things you always forget.Meta's own Muse page encourages users to connect email, calendars, Instagram and other everyday apps. Its Mac application can, with permission, work with files, Messages, Calendar, and Notes. Plaid is providing connections to financial accounts so Muse can offer personalised financial assistance. Meta says 1Password integration is coming. There are more than 2000 connected integrations already. That sounds terrifying when you write it as a list, but it also sounds exactly like what a useful personal agent would need.And this is where I think Meta deserves more credit than some of the current commentary gives it. Muse runs inside a dedicated secure virtual machine, and they say credentials are stored separately so the model itself can’t see them. Sensitive actions such as sending an email or making a purchase require approval so at least there is an audit trail.Users apparently can control individual connections. Meta says Muse conversations and the data stored in the VM are not passed to its advertising systems, and a more strongly encrypted Confidential VM is planned in which even Meta would not be able to access the contents.Those are not trivial protections, but they do not make the strategic implication any smaller. Because Meta does not need to secretly shove your Gmail inbox into an advertising model for Muse to become enormously valuable to Meta. It merely needs Muse to become the place where you go when you want something done. That is why they are running a different race at the moment.This is where the burner-account problem gets weird.We have spent the last decade learning to fragment ourselves online.There is the work email, personal email, spam email, and the email created because some website demanded one. There is the public Instagram, and then the private Instagram and the account you use to look at things you would rather not train your public algorithm on.Meta itself recognised this behaviour years ago; yep, they were all over it. Facebook now allows users to create up to four additional personal profiles under their main account specifically so different interests and communities can remain separate and, of course, not to tie your alter egos to yourself. WhatsApp can remain separate from Meta's broader account system, although users can voluntarily connect it. In 2026, Meta began rolling Accounts Center into a broader Meta Account designed to manage apps and devices under one identity system. That all makes sense in the social-media era, but… the agent era creates the opposite incentive.A privacy-conscious user may decide to give an AI agent a secondary email address, a limited calendar, a burner profile, and only a carefully sanitised slice of their life. I know I do it that way. But I’m continually told that every layer of separation makes the agent slightly more stupid.It can’t remind you about the restaurant reservation buried in the other inbox. It can’t realise that tomorrow's meeting conflicts with the dentist because the dentist is on another calendar. It can’t understand that the person emailing you is the same person appearing in your WhatsApp conversations. It cannot optimise your spending if it only sees one account, and it certainly can’t see that you’ve already dated and blocked that one person on another dating app.So we are heading towards a fascinating identity problem. At what point does the account you trust with your inbox, calendar, relationships, purchases, finances, and personal history become your real account? Are these becoming a series of best on which combination and stack works best? I certainly don’t want to get arrested in 20 years for trading Lima beans on a black-market lookmaxxing site, because unlike burner email accounts, burner agent-connected accounts decide they want to ‘live on’.Maybe the future "real account" isn't Facebook, Google, an email address, etc.; maybe it is an agent. The account with the richest authenticated context about you and permission to operate on your behalf may eventually matter more than the hundred accounts sitting underneath it, but hey, that’s a very different internet.And then there is the slightly absurd AI contradiction.For several years, the public has simultaneously been told that artificial intelligence may be the most dangerous technology humanity has ever created. This whole AI doomer thing is already getting old, but it’s certainly occupying its fair share of space on mediums like the dying New York Times.Researchers discuss alignment and Governments discuss catastrophic risk. AI companies publish preparedness frameworks and meltdown philosophical crisis papers, thinly veiled and geared toward regulatory capture. Meta's own Advanced AI Scaling Framework explicitly evaluates risks including cyber capabilities, biological threats, and potential loss of control.Then the consumer product arrives and essentially says, hold my beer, I’m going to need access to all the things you use, own, frequent, and operate, and I want to be able to fill things out, buy things, work while you are asleep, and do all the things that could actually expedite the very thing that feeds the fears.That contrast is one of the most bonkers things I have seen in my ample years on the blue marble.I don't necessarily think it is a bad thing. In fact, I suspect ordinary consumers may eventually reach a more pragmatic conclusion about AI than much of the industry has. People have always traded some degree of control for enough utility. We gave smartphones our locations because maps became useful. We gave cloud services our photographs because having every photograph on every device was useful.We stored our credit cards in browsers because typing sixteen digits repeatedly became annoying. Agents will probably cross the same line. Let’s face it, we are VERY good at creating lies to ourselves about those trade-offs, and we are excellent at saying, “ah, it will be OK”.But it is entirely reasonable for someone to look at the wider AI safety conversation and ask why, if the machines are supposedly one capability jump away from becoming HAL 9000, the onboarding screen would ask permission to access their bank account. The industry has never completely reconciled those two messages, and Meta is simply making the contradiction visible.Zuckerberg may have learned which race actually matters.There is another reason I think Muse matters. Zuckerberg has spoken openly about Meta's historic strategic weakness: it did not control the dominant computing platforms underneath its products.In a 2025 conversation with Stripe co-founder John Collison, Zuckerberg said that if Meta arrived at the next computing platform at roughly the same time as Apple, Google or Microsoft, the incumbents would have the advantage because they already possessed the underlying ecosystem. His conclusion was that Meta needed to be earlier and better.That helps explain the enormous investment in glasses, and it also somewhat helps to explain Muse.Yesterday Meta announced that Muse is coming to its AI glasses. The progression starts to make sense: social graph, messaging, recommendation engine, AI assistant, personal agent, persistent identity, then an ambient hardware device that can see and hear the world alongside you.Meta isn’t gunning for the best chatbot; they are trying very hard not to spend the next computing era living inside somebody else's operating system. So all eyes are on attention.The moat can’t be only about data. It is the feedback loop.People often say Meta possesses enormous amounts of data, which is obviously true but not particularly insightful because we all know the more important advantage is what happens to the data after it arrives.Meta sees enormous volumes of human behavior. Its models use that behavior to improve recommendations, because better recommendations increase engagement and more engagement creates more behavioral signals. Those signals improve advertising and personalization, and then those improvements attract businesses and creators, who create more things for people to interact with, and now they are putting a personal agent inside that loop.Meta has already said interactions with Meta AI can be used as another recommendation signal across connected Meta accounts. Ask Meta AI about hiking and, under the policy introduced in 2025, that interest can help shape the content and ads you see elsewhere within the Meta ecosystem. Muse itself, ‘they say,’ is treated differently; Meta says its VM data and conversations are not shared with the ad system, but the broader strategic direction toward AI-mediated personalisation could hardly be clearer.The doomers will be quick to state that Meta built an AI to steal more information about you. There really isn't evidence for that claim.The flip-side version would be that Meta has built an AI that becomes more useful the more accurately it understands you, while Meta already owns one of the largest identity, attention, and distribution networks ever constructed.I, for one, don’t need to be tricked into giving it context, but I have to make a decision on whether the utility of the offering is great enough for me to volunteer my information. That is a much better business for them to run, and a much smarter race to try and win.This is the 4D chess move.Muse may become the world's dominant personal agent, or, yeah, it may not.Google has some very tip-top advantages of its own, and OpenAI has massive consumer mindshare. Anthropic is strong in professional and enterprise workflows, and Apple controls some of the world's most valuable consumer hardware. Personal agents remain unreliable, security is difficult, and consumer trust is far from guaranteed.Meta's not-so-squeaky-clean history means some people will quite rationally be more cautious about handing it access to sensitive information. Reuters reported this week that even an experimental Muse feature using human contractors to complete some phone calls generated internal privacy concerns.Meta doesn’t need to win over all the Frontier-AI obsessed people and declare Muse the winner. The people swapping models every fortnight are interesting, vocal and disproportionately visible online. They are not three and a half billion people.Meta's advantage is that it already knows how to reach everybody else and in a language they all understand.The company can survive losing a benchmark or a model arriving six weeks late. It can survive somebody on X declaring its AI strategy dead before breakfast. It has done something similar through mobile, Stories, Reels, messaging, short-form video and multiple rounds of technological panic. It is a king of dying fast and not skipping a beat.What it can’t afford is to lose control of the interface through which billions of ordinary people encounter the next generation of computing. Muse suggests Zuckerberg understands that perfectly.The only question that will ever matter is who owns the relationship between the intelligence and the human being using it.And, eventually, which account the human considers to be the one that actually represents them. If that becomes the real AI race, Meta didn't arrive late at all because it’s been standing on the starting grid for twenty years.

item.title: Publishing on HackerNoon Is a Badge You Get to Keep
item.author: Editing Protocol
item.content:encoded: A few weeks ago, we came across a video from a developer walking through the CV that helped take him from Lagos to London.His name is Pleasant Balogun. He started coding as a teenager, built his first tools using his mom’s Android phone, launched products, had companies acquire his work, and eventually qualified for the UK’s Global Talent route.But there was one small part of his story that caught our attention.Back in 2021, Pleasant won HackerNoon Contributor of the Year for Developer Tools.Looking back on it in his video, Pleasant said the recognition “contributed to… everything downstream.” He then went on to talk about the projects, companies, acquisitions, and experience that eventually formed the application that took him to London.Now, before anyone starts rewriting their immigration plans around their HackerNoon profile: we are not saying a HackerNoon award got Pleasant his UK visa.He doesn’t say that either.What his story does show is something we think writers sometimes underestimate:Putting your work somewhere credible creates receipts.Anyone can create a HackerNoon account and submit a story, but not every submission makes it to publication. Every story goes through editorial review, and as we’ve written before, roughly 60% of the stories that enter our editorial queue don’t make the cut.That selectivity matters because when you publish something useful, technical, original, or genuinely insightful, you’re doing more than adding another post to the internet. You’re creating a public record of what you knew, what you built, what you believed, or the problems you could solve at a particular point in your career.That record can take on different forms of value over time. Six months later, it might be something you send to a recruiter; two years later, it could help establish your expertise; and five years later, it might sit in your portfolio alongside the projects, jobs, awards, conference talks, and open-source contributions you’ve accumulated along the way.You rarely know which piece of work will matter most in the future, and Pleasant probably didn’t either.Look Around at Who You’re Publishing Next ToThere’s another part of publishing on HackerNoon that’s easy to miss when you’re staring at an empty draft: the community you’re joining.That’s the community you’re entering when you hit submit: not one where every writer works at Microsoft, Amazon, or the next billion-dollar startup, and certainly not one where job titles automatically make someone’s ideas better. HackerNoon has always been a place for people building technology to explain what they’re seeing, often before the rest of the industry has completely caught up.You might be reading an engineer solving a production problem at massive scale, a founder building a company nobody has heard of yet, or a 17-year-old creating something on his mom’s phone. The point is that you don’t always know who someone is going to become, and you don’t need to know their title to recognize that they have something worth sharing.Publish Before You Think You’re “Qualified”This is probably the bigger lesson: a lot of people wait until they have the impressive title, the successful startup, the senior role, or the decade of experience before they feel qualified to write publicly. But building a body of work is often what helps them get there in the first place.Write about something you built, explain the weird bug you spent three days solving, or document an experiment that failed. Make the argument everyone on your team keeps having, or share a technical decision you’d make differently today. Your first article doesn’t need to establish you as the world’s foremost expert; it just needs to show that you have something real to contribute.That work can compound in unexpected ways. A side project becomes a job interview, a GitHub repository catches the attention of a founder, or an article becomes proof that you understood a technology years before it became fashionable. Even a HackerNoon award can become a line on your CV that’s still worth talking about five years later.You can’t predict where any of this will lead, but you can give your work a better chance of being discovered by putting it somewhere people can find it.So, if you’ve been sitting on an idea because you don’t think your name is big enough yet, remember that the people whose names seem big today had to publish their first piece somewhere, too.Want to take this further? (HackerNoon’s Blogging Course)HackerNoon’s Blogging Course is designed for beginners writers who’ve published a bit and want to level up. It’s organized into 8 modules created by experienced writers and editors, and it includes topics like:Until next time, Hackers! 💚

item.title: A 1960 Paper Published In Science Predicts World Will End Next Month
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
sciencehabit shares a report from Science Magazine: A physicist has put a definite date on Doomsday," The New York Times wrote on November 4, 1960. "He calculates that it will come on Friday the Thirteenth in November, 2026 A. D. On that date, or thereabouts, the human population will have expanded so far as to approach infinity and thus will automatically annihilate itself." The newspaper was right -- but the prediction was wrong. That week, Austrian American physicist Heinz von Foerster and two colleagues published a paper in Science with the stunningly succinct title "Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026."
The work was based on a simple observation: The time it took for the human population to double in size kept getting shorter. Using population estimates from about 400 B.C.E. until 1958 C.E., the authors -- all from the department of electrical engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign -- came up with an equation that best described the trend. If things continued the way they were going, the number of humans on Earth would rise faster and faster, reaching more than 25 billion by 2020. The researchers didn't calculate when humanity would run out of food, land, or energy. They just concluded that at some point this year, the equation ceased to give meaningful results because the predicted population shot toward infinity. That was their doomsday. "Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve," they wrote. "They will be squeezed to death."
The exact date was somewhat arbitrary, however. The formula solved to 2026.87 plus or minus 5.5 years, and The New York Times reported that von Foerster "searched the center of this doom-time span for an appropriate date and found that a Friday the Thirteenth would fall conveniently in November of 2026." (November 13 also happened to be his birthday.) [...] [D]emographers, annoyed by what they saw as a provocation by outsiders, pointed out obvious flaws. For example, the time it takes for the number of humans to double could get a lot shorter, but certainly not shorter than the 9 months it takes for a baby to develop. "In view of the comments that subsequently were published in this journal, an extensive discussion of this article does not seem to be required," public health expert Harold Dorn drily noted in Science 2 years after von Foerster's article was published. The forecast would set a record, he predicted, "for the short length of time required to demonstrate its unreliability." "The failure of the Doomsday equation is ultimately a cautionary tale about the dangers of extrapolating from historically exceptional circumstances," writes economist Javier Birchenall of the University of California, Santa Barbara writes in a Perspective published in Science today.

item.title: CDC Tools With the Most Predictable Pricing for High-Volume Data Pipelines
item.author: Pipelineguy
item.content:encoded: The most predictable pricing for CDC solutions comes from a billing unit your team can reasonably forecast. For instance:: Estuary and Google Cloud Datastream: Airbyte Pro: Confluent CloudFor high-volume pipelines, this can matter more than any quoted base cost. After all, costs can scale depending on data volume, the number of active rows, events, processing capacity, compute consumption, or even the infrastructure needed to run the pipeline.Keep in mind, though, that pricing predictability doesn’t necessarily mean pricing. It simply refers to the ability to predict how your costs will change as your workload grows.Estuary is particularly interesting because its cloud pricing is based on data that’s been moved and connector task hours, with no MAR pricing and no requirement to run a separate Kafka stack for CDC.What Makes CDC Pricing Predictable?The simplest approach to pricing isn’t always the simplest to predict.If a PostgreSQL database generates 500 GB of modifications this month, but next month, transaction volume doubles, Snowflake is added as another destination, and one large table needs to be backfilled, what will happen to the bill?Well, that’s the million-dollar question. Literally.With volume pricing, the first thing to consider is the number of bytes processed. MAR pricing is more closely related to the number of rows that have been changed. Event-based pricing focuses on inserts, updates, and deletes, whereas capacity-based pricing works differently because the cost stays the same until the system has reached its capacity.Compute-based services add another variable. An increase in traffic can cause a serverless CDC service to go up, even when the average volume per month is relatively unchanged.This gives us several ways to evaluate pricing predictability:How well does the spending align with the amount of data being ingested?What happens if row churn increases?Does adding a new destination create additional charges?Are initial loads and backfills priced separately?How are traffic spikes handled?Does this tool require Kafka, storage, monitoring, or other external infrastructure services?Backfills are not uncommon occurrences, and as such, they deserve particular attention. Teams run them when they add destinations, fix transformations, recover from failures, and integrate new use cases. According to Estuary’s guide to evaluating CDC solutions for 2026 (), they should also be tested along with traffic bursts, destination slowdowns, and backlog recovery.As mentioned in the intro, price comparisons can be difficult when each vendor presents its pricing in a different way.That’s why we looked at each vendor’s pricing model first and identified exactly what it meters, whether it’s the size of data, number of rows/events/connector operations, or infrastructural capacity.Then, we focused on the technical architecture, common use cases, and discussion on platforms like Reddit. However, keep in mind that these discussions are anecdotal. They can help identify potential issues or unexpected charges reported by engineers, but they aren’t a substitute for official pricing information.In short, these are the factors we took into account during our evaluation:Performance at heavy loadsCost of multiple destinationsInfrastructure requirements: This piece was written by Estuary. We know more about Estuary than any other product. Information on other platforms comes from recent vendor documentation and public user feedback.The table below highlights the pricing model for CDC used in each tool and the primary cost driver as the workload increases.Data volume and task hoursGB moved and connector runtimeBillable data at both capture and materialization levelsVolume-based on Standard; capacity-based on ProData volume or data workersTeams looking for managed and capacity-based ingestionCapacity must still be sized for concurrency.Data processed by DatastreamBytes processed may differ significantly from raw source size.Service cost is based on capacity and usage time.Records inserted, updated, and deletedWorkloads with measurable event ratesHigh change rates increase event consumption.Unique active rows per connectionLow-maintenance managed ingestionRow churn and connection structure affect MAR.Compute, tasks, throughput, storage, networkingArchitecture built around KafkaTotal price is a sum of several factors.Infrastructure and engineeringTeams with existing streaming infrastructureA free license doesn't mean free CDC service.As you can see, you can’t compare these values using a single "$ per GB” column.Since the above-mentioned tools have quite different pricing models, it is necessary to know what each tool measures and how the cost varies with the increase in CDC load.: Managed CDC at high volumes where data volume is easier to predict than row-level activity.Estuary’s pricing is fairly simple. It charges $0.50 per GB captured and $0.50 per GB delivered to each destination. So, when 1 GB enters Estuary and 1 GB is delivered to a destination, the data usage portion of the bill is $1.Connector pricing is based on the number of active connector instances. The first six active connector instances cost around $100 per month each. Additional connector instances are $50 per month, prorated based on usage. Keep in mind that both captures and materializations count as connector instances. For BYOC and private cloud deployments, annual pricing plans and additional infrastructure costs apply.In simple terms: data usage + connector instances usageBoth parts are relatively easy for a data engineer to monitor. When billable GBs double while the pipeline configuration stays the same, then the data usage cost also doubles. However, twice as many database updates don’t necessarily mean twice as many bytes. The relevant metric, therefore, is billable data volume, not the number of changes.One architectural detail becomes important when pipelines branch out. Estuary separates data capture from delivery:Capture > Collections > MaterializationsA single capture occurs in collections, which in turn supply multiple destinations. Imagine PostgreSQL needs to stream into Snowflake, S3, and an operational database. There’s no need to pull from the source three times. A new materialization can simply reuse the data that Estuary has captured earlier. The additional destination will move data, but it doesn’t require another historical extraction from the production database.This is significant for both pipeline management and cost. It also eliminates the need for Kafka, Kafka Connect, and connector management separately for teams that want managed CDC.Real-world use cases from Estuary customers show how this works in practice. Xometry reports reducing data integration expenses by more than 60% with pay-as-you-go pricing. Glossier managed to cut their integration costs by 50%, with no unexpected fees. And Cosuno’s pipeline turned out to be 50% less expensive than its previous solution powered by Fivetran.There are also Reddit discussions around rising Fivetran costs and Estuary as an alternative. Though these are useful for understanding how some data engineers view volume-based pricing, I wouldn’t treat reported savings on Reddit as reliable evidence.Estuary has fewer connectors than some of its competitors, and Private/BYOC deployments are associated with additional business and technical concerns. It’s important to consider both the data sources and destinations when making these comparisons.: Teams that require sources/destinations that are not part of the Estuary catalog of connectors, or teams that require general-purpose SaaS ELT more than CDC.: Teams that prefer either the pay-per-use or capacity-based pricing model.Airbyte currently offers two main pricing models. The Standard plan is a fully managed, volume-based product. Airbyte Pro uses data workers in its capacity-based approach. One data worker can handle approximately three simultaneous syncs, depending on the pipelines being run.The advantages of the latter are very easy to grasp. If your pipeline processes additional data for a limited period but stays within its existing capacity, you don’t incur extra charges per GB.However, the problem starts when concurrency or complexity of your workload exceeds your capacity. At that point, you need to add more data workers.The forecasting question is no longer, “What’s the volume of the data transfer?” but “What’s the processing capacity our pipelines will require?”The Pro tariff is quote-based, so the pricing page explains the model using plenty of details rather than mere dollar amounts.Airbyte also offers a self-hosted option..This changes the cost equation considerably because your engineering team is now in control of the platform.In a recent discussion on r/dataengineering, some engineers described self-hosting as cheap and easy, while others reported issues with maintenance and reliability. Another user mentioned saving a significant amount of money annually with Airbyte self-hosted on Kubernetes.These examples clearly demonstrate the actual trade-off: although self-hosting can reduce software costs, the operational work remains your team’s responsibility.: Those who’d like little involvement in operations and don’t want to measure capacity sizing, self-hosting management, or reliability of the connector.3. Google Cloud Datastream: GCP projects looking for managed CDC with volume-based pricing.At a glance, Datastream looks like the simplest option. Google bills for GiBs processed. Volume tiers apply, so the price per GiB decreases as usage increases. Backfilling historical data is billed separately, with the first 500 GiB per month free, according to Google’s current pricing page.There’s an important caveat, though. GiBs processed by Google aren’t always the same as the GiBs from the source database. As noted on Google’s documentation page, internally processed data may be up to 2 to 5 times larger than the actual data for many use cases.That means per-GiB pricing is only as predictable as the definition of the GiB being measured.While Datastream itself doesn’t charge anything beyond the processed volume of data, a full-fledged GCP pipeline might use a variety of additional services, such as Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Dataflow, networking, and more. So, even though Datastream’s own pricing meter is relatively simple, the total cost of a GCP-based CDC pipeline can involve several separate cost centers.: Teams that use multi-cloud architecture and processes where increasing the number of bytes and GCP services makes cost harder to estimate.: Migration and replication workloads on AWS.AWS charges for replication capacity rather than rows or per-GB of changed data.With provisioned DMS, users choose the replication instances and can incur additional charges for extra log storage should they opt for it.DMS Serverless uses DCUs (DMS Capacity Units) as the unit of capacity measurement. 1 DCU corresponds to 2 GB of RAM, and AWS automatically scales the capacity of DMS Serverless, depending on the number of transactions performed.This makes DMS Serverless more flexible but less predictable. AWS can add or decrease capacity as the workload changes, so bursts of replication activity can result in higher DCU usage. The good thing is that AWS allows users to set a maximum number of DCUs, which provides some control over costs.This pricing model makes sense for teams that already run their infrastructure on AWS. However, if the question is something along the lines of “How many GB of CDC do we need?” translating that metric into the compute capacity DMS will need is far from straightforward.: Companies that want a simple volume-based pricing strategy or a CDC solution independent of the AWS ecosystem.: Companies with a predictable rate of database changes that can be estimated based on events.Hevo operates on an event-driven model. According to the company’s documentation, billable actions include record insertions, modifications, and deletions made after creating the pipeline. Deleted source records are counted as updates for billing purposes.This makes pricing closely tied to the amount of change activity. So, if your PostgreSQL database generates 20 million changed records each month, it should be relatively easy to make predictions for the following one.However, the problem appears when the nature of the workload changes. A single bulk update for millions of records is going to generate a large number of events, even if the overall database size hasn’t changed much.Here are two useful points to keep in mind about Hevo’s current consumption pricing at large volumes:Historical data loads are marked as free, and pricing is applied only to the changed data.The unit price goes down when the volume increases, and Hevo provides capacity commitments.Hevo recommends running the workload for four or five days, calculating the average number of events per day, multiplying it by 30, and adding around 5-10% variance.This highlights an important point about event-based pricing: it’s highly dependent on the stability of your event rate.: Processes that experience fluctuating rates of events, large-scale changes, or sudden surges in inserts, updates, and deletions.: Teams that want managed data ingestion and can reliably predict Monthly Active Rows (MAR).Fivetran uses MAR as its primary measure of connection usage.Now, one of the most important words here is . You’re not charged for the byte size of your table. Usage is actually determined based on the number of rows that become through inserts, updates, and deletes. In other words, the same row modified multiple times during a month counts as one MAR charge.Basically, higher synchronization frequency won’t affect the standard MAR as long as the same rows are being updated. Fivetran measures MAR usage based on unique row modifications and not on the number of sync operations.However, keep in mind that History Mode uses a different calculation that takes the number of changes into account. In most cases, though, initial historical syncs are free from MAR charges, while the pricing policy introduced in March 2025 allows historical resyncs to be excluded from paid MAR under certain conditions.So what makes MAR forecasts hard then?One factor is row churn. If your workload touches a significantly larger number of distinct rows, MAR can increase even when the total volume of data changes very little.Another thing is the connection structure. Fivetran now applies its usage curve at the connection level. Two connections that replicate the same source to two destinations will each have their own MAR.The 2025 shift to connection-level tiering helps explain some of the community feedback around Fivetran pricing. One user in a recent r/dataengineering thread mentioned their monthly bill doubled after the changes in pricing. Another user explained their increase was small since the majority of connectors had processed over one million MAR in a month.This explanation is much more informative than simply saying "Fivetran is expensive". As you can see, it all depends on the account structure itself.According to Fivetran, the 2025 pricing change was designed in such a way that accounts with a lot of similar connections would experience increases in price, whereas those that use one large connection would see reductions. Connections with an output of 1 to 1 million paid MAR are subject to a minimum connection fee as of January 2026. Inserts, updates, and deletes all contribute to paid MAR.And there’s another way for larger customers to avoid unpredictability: Fivetran provides Enterprise License Agreements with a fixed annual fee in certain cases.MAR is therefore not inherently unpredictable. It remains relatively predictable when row activity is stable.: Systems with high row churn or independent connections where the use of MAR is more difficult to predict.: Businesses that already have Kafka and event streaming on their platform.Confluent approaches CDC from a stream-processing perspective. Usage-based fully managed connectors are primarily charged based on two measurements:Number of tasks performed per hourData transfer throughput per GBThis applies to the Connect component alone, though. Kafka clusters can also incur compute, networking, and storage expenses, while other Confluent services such as Flink have their own usage metrics.Hence, there is no single measurement that determines the cost, but that’s not necessarily a bad thing.If Kafka already serves as the backbone for your company events, these new offerings might just be the infrastructure you were looking for. It’s just that budgeting requires more information than a simple line item or GB tracker.Confluent has also focused on making this model more predictable. In August 2026, the company unveiled Connect Advantage bundles that allowed companies with consistent usage to make a minimum monthly commitment in exchange for lower-priced connectors and less variance in pricing. As you can see, predictable pricing isn’t synonymous with the pay-as-you-go model. Sometimes, predictability involves making a commitment.: Those teams that only need CDC from databases to warehouses and require no broader use.: Those teams that have been using Kafka or need total control over the CDC stack.Debezium is unlike the other managed products listed here because it’s open source. As such, its licensing terms are very straightforward. It’s also free, but its ecosystem is not.A typical Debezium implementation relies on Kafka Connect:In its own documentation, Debezium identifies Kafka Connect as its most popular configuration. For a production-ready solution, however, you also need to account for Kafka brokers, Connect workers, storage, replication, monitoring, upgrades, scaling, and sink connectors.Debezium can also run in alternative configurations, such as Debezium Engine, which does not require any Kafka or Kafka Connect. However, as stated in documentation, the embedded lightweight version is more fragile and the application needs to take care of the state management that Kafka would normally provide.This trade-off can be observed in community discussions as well. Those engineers, who already work with Kafka, perceive Debezium as a good CDC solution. However, others remark that Kafka operations, scalability problems, and the learning curve may prove to be a challenge. As a r/dataengineering user put it: "Debezium itself is pretty easy to operate, but Kafka consumes the lion’s share of operation effort." There was also a thread discussing how this combination could be difficult to implement if the team planned to scale fast.The better analogy would be:Debezium = free; Debezium license = free; production CDC infrastructure = your responsibility.: Teams without Kafka expertise or experienced operations staff that want someone else to manage their CDC.Pricing Behavior in High-Volume PipelinesLet’s put this into practice. Imagine the following scenario:PostgreSQL as a source database1 TB of changed data per monthBillions of rows of changed dataSnowflake as the first targetOccasional multi-terabyte backfill of historical dataPeak periods that reach three times the normal workloadThen the team decides to add S3 as an additional destination. The value of data han’t changed just because of the pricing model.But pricing behavior could be drastically different.Direct impact if more unique rows changeCan add MAR when another connection is requiredOften treated separately/free under current Fivetran rulesDepends on unique rows modifiedHistorical loading may be treated differentlyMay fit existing capacityMay fit until workers saturateMay require additional capacityCan consume more capacityMay temporarily need more capacityUsually requires more runtime/capacityUsually requires more processingAdditional replication workAutoscaling can increase usageRequires more throughput/storage/consumersCompute + storage + engineeringCapacity planning becomes your jobThat’s because the advertised starting price rarely tells the whole story. What matters is whether you can reliably forecast the metric the pricing model uses to calculate your bill.Platform pricing is only one part of CDC expenses.Debezium is a good example. It doesn’t have a licensing fee, but can still require Kafka brokers, Kafka Connect workers, storage, network, upgrades, and engineering.Cloud-native services incur similar costs. Datastream could be billed by processed GiB, but destination and transformation route may require the use of BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Dataflow, and networking. And even though DMS might not incur a separate charge for its data transfer between nodes within some AWS paths, it does feature costs related to replication instances, serverless capacity, storage, and AWS infrastructure.Don’t forget about destination costs, either. Processing increased number of changes in Snowflake, BigQuery, or other warehouse systems can mean additional compute or storage costs, even when the CDC provider itself charges only a small amount for the additional data.And finally, engineering time. Someone needs to track replication lag, fix connectors following source database upgrade, and manage expired PostgreSQL WAL, Kafka capacity, schema changes, or backfilling failure. While a managed platform would incur these costs in a more transparent way as software billing, self-managed approach will make them a part of cloud expenses and salary.None of these options is less expensive.A proper cost comparison should cover the entire pipeline.When evaluating CDC pricing, use your own workload to estimate what you’ll actually pay.Here are 7 metrics to start with.Measure the amount of CDC data that’s produced daily or monthly from the source. For PostgreSQL, it would be best to measure the WAL throughput rate, which gives you a more accurate view of the actual volume of changes being made.Don’t use database storage volume as an estimate. A 5TB database changing 20GB per day is fundamentally different from 500GB database that is continuously changing.2. Measure Changed Rows or EventsFor MAR- or event-based pricing, calculate number of inserts/updates/deletes.Also, track number of changed unique rows, since that’s important when calculating Monthly Active Rows.3. Distinguish Average Volume from Peak VolumeAn average of 20 MB/s doesn’t tell you much if there are also peaks of 100 MB/s every Friday.They both matter in capacity and serverless compute pricing, so track them both.4.
